title: Intraoperative demonstration of a check-valve mechanism in a spinal extradural arachnoid cyst with nerve root incarceration.
abstract: Spinal extradural arachnoid cysts (SEDACs) are rare lesions thought to arise from a dural defect associated with a check-valve mechanism, although direct intraoperative evidence is limited. We report a 17-year-old female presenting with persistent low back pain and bilateral lower extremity numbness. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a cystic lesion at the Th12-L1 level displacing the dural sac, while computed tomography myelography failed to identify a communicating tract. Surgical exploration was performed due to persistent symptoms and a suspected dynamic mechanism. Intraoperatively, a dural defect at the nerve root sleeve with nerve root incarceration was identified. Cerebrospinal fluid leakage ceased after closure of the defect, confirming a check-valve mechanism. The cyst was resected and the defect repaired. The patient's symptoms resolved completely, with no recurrence at 2-year follow-up. This case provides direct intraoperative evidence of the proposed pathophysiology of SEDAC.

title: MYCN-amplified spinal ependymoma: a three-patient case series and focussed literature review.
abstract: MYCN-amplified spinal ependymomas are a rare, recently described aggressive subtype of ependymoma defined by molecular profiling. We present three cases: a 52-year-old man, a 37-year-old woman, and a 28-year-old man presented with progressive neurological symptoms and spinal cord lesions identified on magnetic resonance imaging. These cases demonstrate the challenges in radiological identification and the importance of histological and molecular profiling to guide aggressive treatment of MYCN-amplified spinal ependymomas including surgical resection, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. Outcomes varied across cases from clinical stability to death, reflecting the heterogeneity of the clinical course. We offer a short literature review to contextualise the cases.

title: Navigated robotic-arm-assisted hybrid multi-portal endoscopic fenestration of a thoracic intradural arachnoid cyst: a technical case report.
abstract: Endoscopic treatment of spinal intradural lesions is technically demanding because bimanual manipulation, irrigation control, neural protection, and dural closure are constrained. A 44-year-old woman with myelopathy from a dorsal T4-T10 intradural arachnoid cyst underwent endoscopic fenestration at T4/5. The hybrid multi-portal technique combined unilateral biportal-style exposure, a uniportal working-channel endoscope, intraoperative navigation, and robotic-arm camera stabilization. An accessory portal enabled bimanual intradural manipulation. Irrigation pressure was reduced after durotomy, and the dura was closed with sutures and clips reinforced by sealants. Day 1 magnetic resonance imaging confirmed cord decompression, and lower-limb sensory and bladder symptoms had resolved at 6 weeks. To our knowledge, this is the first reported navigated robotic-arm-assisted hybrid multi-portal endoscopic fenestration of a thoracic intradural arachnoid cyst. This single case demonstrates technical feasibility but not superiority over open or microscopic surgery.

title: Evaluation of urine clusterin and cystatin B concentrations in relation to histopathologic findings of renal disease in dogs.
abstract: Background Conventional markers of kidney disease detect altered kidney function but do not consistently identify active kidney injury. Urine clusterin (uClust) and cystatin B (uCysB) are renal injury biomarkers, but their evaluation is limited in dogs with biopsy-confirmed diagnoses. Hypothesis/objectives Determine the association of uClust and uCysB with conventional biomarkers, category of renal disease, severity of renal injury, and survival in dogs with biopsy-confirmed kidney disease. Animals Urine from client-owned dogs (n = 199) submitted to the International Veterinary Renal Pathology Service between 2008 and 2018 with corresponding kidney biopsy samples. Methods Retrospective study. Urine clusterin and uCysB were measured using an ELISA, and correlations with serum creatinine (sCr), symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPC), and histopathology severity scores were determined. Significant differences in uClust and uCysB among conventional biomarker groups were determined using analysis of variance. Multivariate survival analysis was performed. Results Concentrations of uClust and uCysB were highest in dogs with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) and mixed MPGN, and they were positively correlated with sCr, SDMA, UPC, and histopathology scores (r = 0.25-0.50). Risk of death was higher in dogs with uCysB > 238 ng/mL (hazard ratio, 2.40; P < .05), whereas uClust > 7329 ng/mL was associated with lower risk of death (hazard ratio, 0.32; P < .01). Conclusions and clinical importance Higher uCysB was associated with more severe disease and decreased survival; therefore, uCysB might identify dogs with active renal injury and worse prognosis. Although uClust was associated with more severe disease, its association with survival needs further investigation.

Higher uCysB was associated with more severe disease and decreased survival; therefore, uCysB might identify dogs with active renal injury and worse prognosis. Although uClust was associated with more severe disease, its association with survival needs further investigation.

title: Metabolomic signatures in synovial tissue characterize osteoarthritis-like phenotypes in rheumatoid arthritis of knee.
abstract: Objective Osteoarthritis-like rheumatoid arthritis (OA-like RA) is a clinical phenotype characterized by suppressed joint destruction and radiographic features mimicking OA, despite an underlying RA diagnosis. This study aimed to elucidate the pathophysiological distinctions among OA-like RA, typical RA, and OA through histopathological and metabolomic profiling of synovial tissues. Methods Twenty-four patients with RA and six with OA undergoing total knee arthroplasty were enrolled. RA cases were classified into two subgroups: OA-like RA (n = 10; predominant osteoarthritic changes) and typical RA (n = 14; classic RA findings). Knee synovial tissues harvested intraoperatively were evaluated using the Krenn score and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS)-based metabolomics. Results Among 475 GC-MS-detectable compounds, 211 metabolites were identified. Although statistical significance was attenuated following false discovery rate correction, nominal p-values identified five candidate metabolites with differential abundance: hydroxyproline (a marker of cartilage degradation) and four energy- and inflammation-related metabolites (sucrose, 2-aminoadipic acid, lactic acid, and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid). While the Krenn synovitis score was numerically higher in the typical RA group, there were no statistically significant differences among the groups. Conclusion This exploratory study provides preliminary metabolomic insights into OA-like RA, warranting larger cohorts to validate these biomarkers and delineate its pathophysiology.

title: Pretherapeutic Tumor Growth Velocity Refines Survival Stratification Beyond Clinical, Molecular, and Surgical Factors in IDH-Mutant Lower-Grade Gliomas.
abstract: Background Contemporary risk stratification of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant lower-grade gliomas relies primarily on molecular characteristics and surgical tumor burden but does not capture dynamic tumor behavior. Our primary objective was to determine whether pretherapeutic tumor growth velocity (TGV) provides independent prognostic information for overall survival (OS) beyond established factors. Methods This multicenter retrospective study included 569 adults with grade 2-3 IDH-mutant gliomas from three French centers, comprising a development cohort (n = 440) and two external validation cohorts (n = 129). TGV was derived from automated, outcome-blinded volumetric analysis of serial preoperative MRI using mean diameter expansion and log-volume growth. Prognostic value was assessed using multivariable Cox regression, external validation, decision curve analysis, and exploratory random survival forests. Results During a median follow-up of 6.8 years, 73 deaths occurred in the development cohort. Higher TGV was independently associated with shorter overall survival after adjustment for age, sex, grade, 1p/19q status, and postoperative residual tumor volume (HR per 1-mm/year increase, 1.046; 95%CI, 1.011-1.083; P=.011), and was independently replicated externally (HR, 1.077; 95% CI, 1.005-1.153; P=.035). Findings were consistent using log-volume growth and after accounting for CDKN2A/B status. Adding TGV improved prognostic model fit (likelihood-ratio χ²=5.70; P=.017), with greatest incremental value in astrocytomas. Decision curve analysis demonstrated additional clinical utility, while survival forests identified TGV among the strongest survival predictors alongside 1p/19q status and postoperative residual tumor volume. Conclusions Pretherapeutic TGV independently predicts survival beyond contemporary molecular and surgical factors in IDH-mutant lower-grade gliomas. This accessible MRI-derived biomarker may refine individualized risk stratification, particularly in astrocytoma.

title: Deciphering the molecular granularity of subependymomas and its distinction from posterior fossa ependymoma.
abstract: Background The CNS tumor classification of the WHO currently subsumes subependymomas (SE) of the supratentorial, infratentorial, and spinal compartment as one tumor type. Molecular data on SE are generally sparse, but SE are known to exhibit distinct global DNA methylation profiles according to their anatomical location. Previous studies indicate that a fraction of posterior fossa tumors exhibiting DNA methylation profiles of SE morphologically appear as ependymomas and may be prone to relapse. Methods We assembled a cohort of ependymal tumors that best match supratentorial (n = 89), infratentorial (n = 146), or spinal (n = 45) SE DNA methylation profiles. Results Infratentorial tumors with an SE DNA methylation profile occurred at significantly higher ages with a male to female ratio of 4:1 and displayed two distinct subtypes. One of them (n = 49) was enriched for tumors that morphologically appear as ependymomas, carrying a loss of chromosome 6 as well as TERT promoter mutations. Respective patients showed a significantly shorter progression-free survival (p = 0.00014). Supratentorial SE frequently showed chromosome 8 loss while a small subset of tumors with a distinct DNA methylation profile and a segmentation of chromosome 6 was detected. Such chromosomal abnormalities were similarly observed in spinal SE. Conclusions Based on clustering analysis and clinical features of tumors best matching a subependymoma methylation class, we postulate four subtypes of subependymomas. A fifth, previously undefined type of infratentorial ependymomas was provisionally named PFC. It showed frequent relapses but was distinct from PFA and PFB ependymomas.

title: Vorasidenib in IDH1/2-mutant low-grade gliomas: a prospective study on volumetric MRI and seizure outcome.
abstract: Background The IDH1/2 inhibitor vorasidenib demonstrated efficacy in residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant gliomas after surgery. However, there is lack of knowledge regarding factors predicting the probability of response. Patients and methods We conducted a prospective single-centre study on 54 grade 2 IDH1/2-mutant astrocytomas and IDH1/2-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas treated with vorasidenib. MRI response (2D and 3D) and seizure outcome were longitudinally assessed. Factors associated with response were explored using regression models. Results With a median follow-up of 17.5 months, vorasidenib induced progressive tumour shrinkage on MRI, with median volume reductions of - 12.2% at cycle 6, -27.8% at cycle 12, and -55.5% at cycle 18. Best volumetric response was CR in 1 patient, PR in 5, MR in 9, SD in 31 and PD in 7. The ORR (CR + PR + MR) was 28%. Eighteen patients who had focal grade 3 areas showed similar volumetric response and ORR. 9/12 (75%) patients with baseline seizures achieved ≥50% reduction or seizure freedom. MRI response correlated with early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction. Vorasidenib was generally well tolerated, with liver enzyme elevation being the main adverse event. Conclusions Vorasidenib induced sustained tumour shrinkage and seizure control. Early treatment initiation and early seizure reduction were associated with MRI response.

title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: A Review in Neuroimaging.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become central to neuro-oncological imaging, impacting clinical and scientific workflows. In clinical practice, AI-based image reconstruction and noise reduction expedite the generation of advanced multiparametric MRI and PET scans. Automated segmentation and volumetric analysis improve reproducibility, speed, and standardization of tumor quantification and response assessment. In research, large language and multimodal models extract structured information from radiology reports and medical records. Collaborative initiatives, such as BraTS and FeTS, have established standardized, privacy-compliant frameworks for large-scale quantitative analyses. Tumor-specific applications include noninvasive molecular profiling in gliomas, grading and recurrence prediction in meningiomas, detection and response assessment in brain metastases, and pediatric-specific modeling aligned with RAPNO. However, AI models remain sensitive to technical and biological variations across institutions, limiting their clinical utility unless appropriate training and validation is performed. Nevertheless, progress is evident in prospective, biopsy-validated infiltration mapping, assessment of resection extent aligned with RANO-Resect, and standardization through AI-RANO. Emerging directions include foundation models, uncertainty estimation, federated learning, AI-enhanced ultra-low-field MRI, and dual-tracer PET. When used as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for the imaging team, AI can increasingly improve the utility, reproducibility, and efficiency of quantitative, multiparametric imaging in patients with brain tumors.

title: Neural Correlates of Smoking Cessation: A Systematic Review of Magnetic Resonance Imaging Studies.
abstract: Tobacco use is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite efficacious interventions, smoking cessation remains difficult for many individuals. While demographic and behavioural predictors of smoking cessation outcomes are well-documented, neurobiological predictors of success have been inconsistent across studies. The current systematic review aimed to identify neuroimaging biomarkers consistently associated with smoking cessation success. A systematic search identified 32 studies that examined neural predictors of outcomes across structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging modalities and intervention types. The most frequently implicated brain regions included the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC), striatum, and anterior insula. Specifically, greater medial PFC response to health promotion tasks; greater reactivity to smoking-related cues in the dorsolateral PFC and dorsal striatum; stronger resting state functional connectivity between the insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, and medial frontal gyrus; and greater global gray matter volume were commonly reported as predictors of better treatment response. The current systematic review identifies the most robust MRI biomarkers of smoking cessation, but in a relatively small overall literature with extensive heterogeneity among studies.

title: Single-session robotic bronchoscopy diagnoses histologically discordant synchronous lung lesions.
abstract: Histologically discordant synchronous pulmonary lesions in a previously treated patient may represent independent primaries, intrapulmonary metastasis, or histologic transformation. A 74-year-old woman with previously treated right upper lobe adenosquamous carcinoma developed two new, spatially separate, solid fluorodeoxyglucose-avid lesions. Both were sampled during one anaesthetic using shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with radial-probe endobronchial ultrasound confirmation. The peripheral right upper lobe lesion was small cell carcinoma; the left upper lobe lesion was non-small cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified, with patchy TTF-1 and p40 expression compatible with adenosquamous differentiation. Comparative clonality testing was not performed, so their relationship remained unproven. Both lesions received stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (50 Gy in five fractions); the small cell carcinoma was also treated with carboplatin and etoposide, with consolidation durvalumab planned. Bilateral sampling revealed clinically consequential histologic heterogeneity and enabled histology-directed therapy without assuming a common origin.

title: Post-surgical ctDNA as a prognostic biomarker for relapse of resected cholangiocarcinoma.
abstract: Background ctDNA is increasingly used to detect minimal residual disease, however, its sensitivity varies by tumor type. Its utility in CCA remains incompletely defined. Methods In this single-institution retrospective study, we evaluated ctDNA using a commercial tumor-informed assay (Signatera), compared with CA19-9, for predicting relapse after surgical resection during postoperative (<90 days) and surveillance (≥90 days) windows. We assessed associations between ctDNA status and clinical features, including resection pathology and sites of radiographic relapse. Results Of 48 patients with CCA who underwent resection between 2020-2025, 26 (54.2%) experienced relapse (median follow-up 18.3 months). ctDNA positivity during both postoperative and surveillance windows was associated with worse median disease-free survival, whereas CA19-9 was not. During the postoperative window, ctDNA sensitivity was 41.7% and specificity was 85.7% for predicting disease relapse any time post-resection. During the surveillance window, sensitivity was 60.0% and specificity was 90.9%. Landmark analysis for relapse at 1-year for ctDNA collected prior to 90 days had a sensitivity of 83.3% and specificity of 90.0%. Among patients with detectable ctDNA who subsequently developed radiographic relapse, median lead time from first ctDNA positivity to relapse was 34 days (IQR 26-132 days), with a maximum lead time of 292 days. ctDNA performance was higher among patients without perineural or lymphovascular invasion and was most frequently positive in those who developed extrahepatic metastases (n = 10/13, 76.9%). Conclusions ctDNA is a specific prognostic biomarker that outperforms CA19-9 for predicting relapse after CCA. However, negative ctDNA results should be interpreted cautiously given modest assay sensitivity.

title: Adaptive deep learning model with anatomical priors for 3D segmentation of fine hepatic vasculature on CT.
abstract: Background Accurate segmentation of fine hepatic vessels on CT remains challenging because peripheral branches are small and low contrast. Purpose To develop and test PriM Fusion Net, a deep learning model that adaptively integrates an optimized anatomical prior to improve 3D CT segmentation of portal and hepatic veins, emphasizing fine peripheral branches for preoperative 3D modeling. Materials and methods This retrospective study used the public Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) Task08-HepaticVessel dataset of 303 abdominal CT volumes. PriM Fusion Net uses a dual-encoder architecture: a Swin Transformer processes CT images and a parallel convolutional pathway processes a dataset-optimized Frangi vesselness prior. Gated multimodal units act as spatially varying voxel-wise gates that fuse the 2 feature streams at multiple scales. A rule-based SimpleMind post-processing module refined anatomical plausibility. Performance was evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and zero-shot external inference on 3DIRCADb (3D Image Reconstruction for Comparison of Algorithm Database). Results PriM Fusion Net achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 77.68% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 77.11, 78.25) and 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 11.55 mm (95% CI, 9.94, 13.16), outperforming all baselines (all adjusted P < .02). For vessels with radius ≤ 1.5 mm, DSC improved by 13.5% versus SwinUNETR (59.2% [95% CI, 54.48, 63.92] vs 45.7% [95% CI, 40.49, 50.91]). In ablation, replacing rigid concatenation with gated fusion improved DSC from 75.86% (95% CI, 75.31, 76.41) to 77.65% (95% CI, 76.92, 78.38), and SimpleMind post-processing reduced HD95 from 14.98 mm (95% CI, 10.91, 19.05) to 11.55 mm (95% CI, 9.94, 13.16). On 3DIRCADb, zero-shot inference yielded DSC of 68.42% (95% CI, 65.82, 71.02) and HD95 of 11.78 mm (95% CI, 8.50, 15.06). Conclusion Adaptive deep fusion of an optimized anatomical prior improved CT segmentation of portal and hepatic veins, especially fine peripheral branches, supporting further evaluation in 3D vascular modeling workflows for liver surgery and intervention.

title: Krebs Von Den Lungen-6 as a biomarker for lung disease activity and diagnosis in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
abstract: Objectives Children with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and lung disease (LD) are at increased risk of serious complications and premature mortality, making early detection and intervention critical. Krebs von den Lungen 6 (KL-6) is a blood-based biomarker for interstitial lung disease in adults; however, its role in pediatric LD is unclear. This study evaluates KL-6 as a discriminatory and disease activity biomarker for sJIA-LD. Methods Thirty-two patients with sJIA-LD were enrolled through the Childhood Arthritis and Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry. Comparators included sJIA patients without LD, children with primary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and healthy control children. Results Median KL-6 levels were significantly higher in sJIA-LD (596.3 U/mL [IQR 273.5-5,896.3]) compared to sJIA without LD (193.0 U/mL [151.0-252.0], p < 0.0001) and healthy controls (171.9 U/mL [89.7-224.3], p = 0.001), with no difference versus PAP (596.3 vs. 1429.9, p = 0.30). A cut-off of 259.5 U/mL yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 80.9% specificity for LD (AUC 0.856, p < 0.0001). At 371.5 U/mL, specificity reached 100% with 68.7% sensitivity and 100% positive predictive value. SJIA-LD features associated with higher median KL-6 levels included oxygen requirement, abnormal pulse oximeter (<90%), and abnormal chest radiographs. KL-6 strongly correlated with physician global assessment of lung disease but not with markers of systemic inflammation or macrophage activation syndrome. Conclusion KL-6 is a useful biomarker for discriminating LD and evaluating disease activity in sJIA-LD. Future efforts should focus on the utility of KL-6 for monitoring disease progression, treatment response, and predicting long-term disease trajectories.

Methods

Thirty-two patients with sJIA-LD were enrolled through the Childhood Arthritis and Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry. Comparators included sJIA patients without LD, children with primary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and healthy control children.

Results

Median KL-6 levels were significantly higher in sJIA-LD (596.3 U/mL [IQR 273.5-5,896.3]) compared to sJIA without LD (193.0 U/mL [151.0-252.0], p < 0.0001) and healthy controls (171.9 U/mL [89.7-224.3], p = 0.001), with no difference versus PAP (596.3 vs. 1429.9, p = 0.30). A cut-off of 259.5 U/mL yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 80.9% specificity for LD (AUC 0.856, p < 0.0001). At 371.5 U/mL, specificity reached 100% with 68.7% sensitivity and 100% positive predictive value. SJIA-LD features associated with higher median KL-6 levels included oxygen requirement, abnormal pulse oximeter (<90%), and abnormal chest radiographs. KL-6 strongly correlated with physician global assessment of lung disease but not with markers of systemic inflammation or macrophage activation syndrome.

Conclusion

KL-6 is a useful biomarker for discriminating LD and evaluating disease activity in sJIA-LD. Future efforts should focus on the utility of KL-6 for monitoring disease progression, treatment response, and predicting long-term disease trajectories.

title: Radiographic Accuracy of Identifying Anterolateral Tibial Plafond Involvement in Pronation External Rotation Ankle Fractures.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the rate of anterolateral tibial plafond involvement in pronation-external rotation (PER) ankle fractures and analyze the accuracy of radiographs, using CT as the reference standard among fractures with paired imaging, in detecting anterolateral tibial plafond involvement, impaction, and predicting surgeons' stated intent to pursue direct visualization and articular reduction, as determined by surgeon assessment of the imaging findings. Methods Design: Multi-institutional retrospective chart review. Setting Two level 1 trauma centers in the United States. Patient selection criteria Adult patients operative treated PER ankle fractures (AO/OTA 44C) from 2020-2022 and adequate preoperative radiographs, defined as an AP, mortise and lateral view of the injured ankle were included. A subset of these patients also had preoperative CT imaging of the injured ankle and were therefore evaluated with both imaging modalities. Outcome measurements and comparisons All images were reviewed by 4 fellowship-trained orthopaedic trauma surgeons. For this study, anterolateral tibial plafond involvement was defined as the presence of any fracture line or impaction involving the anterolateral plafond, and impaction (a subset of involvement) as where the anterolateral plafond was crushed and depressed. A finding was considered present if at least 3 of the 4 reviewers indicated its presents on first-round responses. The rates of involvement and impaction were determined among all fractures based on radiographs alone, and separately among the subset of patients with paired radiographs and CT. Using CT as the gold standard, we determined the accuracy of radiographs and compared surgeons' stated intent to pursue direct visualization and articular reduction of the anterolateral plafond fracture before versus after review of CT imaging. Results Eighty-three PER ankle fractures were included (mean age 43.3 years [range, 17-89]; 63.9% male), of which 37 also had CT scans (mean age 39.2 years [range, 17-83]; 73.0% male). Among all 83 fractures, anterolateral tibial plafond involvement and impaction were identified on radiographs in 14.5% and 4.8% of cases, respectively. Among the 37 PER ankle fractures with both plain radiographs and CT scans, anterolateral plafond involvement was identified in 13.5% of radiographs versus 37.8% of CT scans (p=0.346) and impaction in 5.4% of radiographs versus 8.1% of CT scans (p=0.005). The diagnosis of impaction using plain radiographs was correct in 66.7% of fractures compared with CT, resulting in a sensitivity of 67%, specificity of 100%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 100%, and negative predictive value (NPV) of 97%. The diagnosis of anterolateral plafond involvement using plain radiographs had a sensitivity of 21%, specificity of 91%, PPV of 60%, and NPV of 66% compared with CT. Plain radiographs predicted surgeons' stated intent to pursue direct visualization and articular reduction in 66.7% of cases and had a PPV of 100% and NPV of 97%. Conclusions In PER ankle fractures, the rates of anterolateral tibial plafond involvement and impaction were 37.8% and 8.1% on CT, respectively. Plain radiographs demonstrated high specificity but limited sensitivity for identifying both impaction (67%) and involvement (21%). Because anterolateral plafond impaction was relatively uncommon in PER fractures, a CT obtained for this purpose alone would yield a positive finding in only a minority of cases; nonetheless, CT should be considered for PER ankle fractures more broadly, given that plain radiographs miss a meaningful proportion of both involvement and impaction and interobserver reliability of radiograph-based assessment was poor. Level of evidence Prognostic level III.

title: Computed Tomography Scan Zone-of-Injury Modeling Predicts Need for Definitive Soft-Tissue Coverage and Complications in Open OTA 42A-C Tibial Shaft Fractures.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the ability of a CT-derived soft-tissue zone-of-injury (ZOI) model to predict the need for soft-tissue (ST) coverage in open 42A-C tibial shaft fractures and compare its discriminatory performance with the Gustilo-Anderson (GA) classification for fracture-related complications. Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Urban, multi-site academic center, 2014-2024. Patient selection criteria Patients with operatively treated open OTA 42A-C tibial shaft fractures, preoperative tibial CT imaging, and ≥6-month follow-up were included. Outcome measures and comparisons The primary outcome was the need for ST coverage (skin-graft, dermal matrix, local flap, free flap, or amputation). Secondary outcomes included ST- and fracture-related complications. CT-derived ZOI measurements, demographics, and injury characteristics were entered into a multivariable regression with stepwise elimination to develop a CT-derived ST coverage model (CTzoi-STC), which was compared with GA classification and with a model without CT-derived data. Patients were further stratified by risk for secondary outcome comparisons. Results 122 patients (40.5 years (range 18-72), 95 (77.9%) male, GA I: 19 (15.6%), II: 30 (24.6%), III: 73 (59.8%); III: 73 (59.8%), of which IIIA: 62 (84.9%), IIIB: 8 (11.0%), IIIC: 3 (4.1%)) met inclusion criteria, with 37 (30.3%) requiring ST coverage. The final CTzoi-STC model, which included longitudinal free air extent on CT scan, wound size, and wound location (tibial third), demonstrated higher discrimination for predicting ST coverage compared with GA classification (AUC 0.845 vs 0.731, p = 0.041). A model without CT-derived data (GA classification, wound size, and wound location) had an AUC of 0.829 (p = 0.654 vs CTzoi-STC). Free air extent remained independently associated with ST coverage after adjustment (OR 8.1, 95% CI 1.4-47.2, p = 0.021). Using the Youden-derived cutoff (0.278), 30 of 47 high-risk patients (63.8%) required ST coverage compared with 7 (9.3%) of low-risk patients. High-risk patients had higher rates of nonunion (40.4% vs 16.0%, p = 0.003), fracture-related infection (38.3% vs 17.3%, p = 0.010), and ST coverage failure (14.9% vs 0.0%, p < 0.001), with longer length-of-stay, more operations and readmissions (all p ≤ 0.006). GA-based stratification showed limited discrimination. Conclusions For open tibial shaft fractures, a CT-derived soft-tissue zone-of-injury model incorporating longitudinal free air extent, wound size, and wound location more accurately identified patients requiring soft-tissue coverage and those at risk for soft-tissue- and fracture-related complications than the Gustilo-Anderson classification. Free air extent on CT was an objective, independent predictor of soft-tissue coverage, although a model without CT-derived data had similar discrimination. Level of evidence III, Prognostic.

title: Effectiveness and Safety of Prophylactic Inferior Vena Cava Filters in High-Risk Hip Fracture Patients: Clinical implications of an early retrieval strategy.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of prophylactic inferior vena cava (IVC) filter in patients with hip fracture who were at high risk for pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE). Methods Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting Single-center Level I Trauma Center. Patient selection criteria Patients older than 50 years who sustained a low-energy hip fracture (AO/OTA 31A, B, and 32A) and underwent prophylactic IVC filter insertion before hip fracture surgery between 2005 and 2025 were included. Prophylactic IVC filter placement was selectively performed in patients with either objectively confirmed deep vein thrombosis on preoperative screening or absolute contraindications to mechanical and pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. Those who had multiple trauma at the time of injury, a clinical follow-up duration ≤6 months after surgery, or undergone IVC filter placement following a confirmed diagnosis of PTE based on pulmonary computed tomography or lung perfusion scanning were excluded. Outcome measures and comparisons The primary outcome was the rate of newly developed symptomatic PTE. Secondary outcomes included IVC filter-related complications, retrieval rates, and 30-day mortality. Results One hundred fifty-six patients were included in the prophylactic IVC filter group (39 men 25.0%], 117 women [75.0%]; mean age, 75.8 ± 11.1 years; femoral neck [AO/OTA 31B], n = 71 [45.5%]; intertrochanteric [31A], n = 75 [48.1%]; subtrochanteric [AO/OTA 32A], n = 10 [6.4%];mean indwelling time, 9.1 days; retrieval rate, 88.5%). Among these patients, no cases of newly developed symptomatic PTE were observed (0%), whereas the incidence in the overall hip fracture cohort (n=4,568) was 0.44%. Filter-related complications occurred in 3.9% of patients (minor tilting, 2.6%; vessel adhesion, 1.3%), with no major mechanical failures such as migration or perforation. Although no thrombi were detected at insertion, 4.5% of the patients had trapped thrombi at the time of removal. The 30-day all-cause mortality rate was 1.3% (2/156) in the prophylactic IVC filter group, compared with 1.5% (67/4,568) in the overall hip fracture cohort. (p=0.845). Neither death in the prophylactic IVC filter group was attributed to PTE or an IVC filter-related complication. Conclusions In this study's selected extreme pulmonary thromboembolism risk cohort, including patients with CT-confirmed preoperative DVT, those clinically expected to undergo prolonged perioperative immobilization, or those with contraindications to prophylactic anticoagulation, such as GI bleeding, prophylactic inferior vena cava filter served as an effective and safe temporary bridge therapy rather than a routine prophylactic strategy. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III.

title: Long-Term Outcomes of 4 Treatment Strategies for Late-Onset Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease.
abstract: Background The age at disease onset is the main prognostic factor in Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD). Onset over 8 years of age is considered an indicator of worse long-term outcomes and need for surgical management to preserve or recover femoral head sphericity. However, no consensus exists on which surgical technique offers the best results. This study aims to compare the long-term radiographic and clinical outcomes of conservative treatment, femoral varus osteotomy (FVO), shelf acetabular osteotomy (SAO), and arthrodiastasis with posteromedial selective epiphysiodesis in late-onset LCPD. Methods All patients with LCPD who had onset after 8 years of age and were followed until skeletal maturity were included. We classified 95 hips into conservative treatment (n=26), FVO (n=26), SAO (n=15), and arthrodiastasis with epiphysiodesis (n=28). Clinical measurements included age, sex, leg-length discrepancy (LLD), and modified Harris Hip Score. Radiographic parameters included Herring classification, Stulberg classification, sphericity deviation score, and residual osteochondritis. Results Patients undergoing arthrodiastasis had better long-term radiographic outcomes, as measured by Stulberg grade (P=0.01) and sphericity deviation score (P=0.04), than those undergoing conservative treatment, FVO, or SAO. Hips undergoing arthrodiastasis developed Stulberg grades IV to V in 39% of cases, compared with 54% in conservatively treated hips, 73% in FVO, and 80% in SAO. Arthrodiastasis patients also had lower final LLD (3.61±5.1 mm, P=0.04) and less residual osteochondritis (11%, P=0.01) than the other groups (average LLD 6.99±7.6 mm, average osteochondritis prevalence 28%), which did not differ between them (P=0.10 and P=0.45, respectively). The modified Harris Hip Score was also significantly higher in arthrodiastasis (95.4±8.4) than in other treatment groups (90.6±11.6, P=0.04). Conclusion Arthrodiastasis with epiphysiodesis is a viable treatment option for late-onset LCPD, with improved long-term radiographic and clinical outcomes compared with other, more aggressive surgical alternatives. Level of evidence Level III-retrospective cohort study.

title: Reliability of Ultrasound-Based Metrics for Patellofemoral Instability: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background Patellofemoral instability (PFI) is a common pediatric knee injury for which imaging plays an important role in risk stratification and treatment planning. Evaluation of anatomic risk factors and associated injuries currently relies on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT). Ultrasound (US) offers several advantages, including dynamic assessment, lack of radiation, portability, and lower cost; however, its role in the evaluation of PFI remains poorly defined. The purpose of this systematic review was to identify and assess reported US-based metrics used to evaluate PFI and investigate their potential incorporation into a standardized imaging protocol. Exclusion criteria included reviews, expert opinions, and nonultrasound or nonpatellofemoral studies. Results The included studies comprised 3263 knees in 1997 patients. title: Machine Learning-based Cluster Analysis Identifies Three Clinically Relevant Phenotypes of Patients With Degenerative Lumbar Scoliosis With Distinct Clinical Profiles and Postoperative Outcomes.
abstract: Study design A retrospective observational study. Objective This study aimed to apply machine learning-based clustering to identify distinct phenotypes of DLS patients with diverse clinical profiles and recovery trajectories. Summary of background data Patients with degenerative lumbar scoliosis (DLS) exhibit substantial heterogeneity in pathology, baseline impairments, frailty, and surgical expectations. However, existing classification systems primarily rely on radiographic parameters and fail to integrate multidimensional patient characteristics, limiting their ability to capture patient heterogeneity and guide individualized surgical strategies. Methods Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed to determine possible patient phenotypes based on a set of screened preoperative demographic, clinical, and radiographic variables. Goodness-of-fit indices were used to determine the optimal cluster number. Baseline and outcome differences among phenotypes were evaluated using analysis of variance and subsequent post hoc Tukey's test. A phenotype classification tool was then established and deployed as a web-based application for clinical use. Results A total of 257 DLS patients were included. Three distinct phenotypes were identified: (1) mild type (n=98, 38.1%), characterized by younger age, minimal deformity, and the most favorable recovery with the lowest dissatisfaction; (2) frailty-dominant type (n=95, 37.0%), defined by advanced age, higher frailty burden, slower recovery, and persistent postoperative pain; and (3) deformity-dominant type (n=64, 24.9%), marked by severe coronal and sagittal malalignment, greater surgical complexity, and the highest rate of postoperative residual coronal malalignment. Across all phenotypes, combined lateral-posterior approaches reduced blood loss and instrumented levels compared with posterior-only approaches. Notably, in frailty-dominant patients, combined approaches further improved early ambulation (46.9% vs. 17.5%, P=0.002) and reduced dissatisfaction (21.9% vs. 44.4%, P=0.031). The phenotype classification tool demonstrated good agreement with the LPA-derived phenotype assignments (F1-score: 0.866). Conclusions Machine learning-based clustering identified three distinct phenotypes of DLS patients. This classification captures the multidimensional heterogeneity of patients with DLS and highlights the importance of phenotype-specific surgical strategies. The accompanying web-based classification tool offers a practical means to integrate these findings into routine clinical practice. Level of evidence III.

title: The Effects of One- and Two-Level Cervical Arthrodesis on Adjacent Segment Center of Rotation During Flexion/Extension at Three Years After Surgery.
abstract: Study design Prospective cohort study. Objective To determine the effects of time since arthrodesis and number of levels fused on the path of the center of rotation (COR) in motion segments adjacent to anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF). We hypothesized the path of the COR in adjacent segments would change up to 3 years post-surgery and be affected more after two-level versus one-level arthrodesis. Summary of background data The location of the COR between adjacent vertebrae reflects the combined translation and rotation that occurs simultaneously during flexion/extension and can be used to infer loading applied to individual motion segments. The path of the COR has been shown to be different among cervical spine motion segments in healthy individuals. Methods Sixty-two arthrodesis patients were tested before surgery and at 1- and 3-years post-surgery. Twenty-two age-matched controls were tested once. All participants performed full range of motion (ROM) flexion/extension while synchronized biplane radiographs were collected at 30 frames per second. A validated volumetric model-based tracking technique was used to determine intervertebral kinematics. The path of the COR was calculated and compared between patients and controls using a linear mixed-effect model. Results The path of the COR at 3 years after two-level arthrodesis at C4/C5/C6 was more anterior in the C3/C4 superior adjacent motion segment compared to controls (P<0.027) and in the C6/C7 inferior adjacent motion segment compared to controls (P<0.04) and one-level arthrodesis patients (P=0.045). No change in COR path was found between pre-operative, one-year or three-years after one- or two-level arthrodesis. Conclusion These in vivo data indicate that 2-level arthrodesis, but not 1-level arthrodesis, affects the way adjacent segments move 3 years after ACDF. Level of evidence Level III.

title: Prediction of Pedicle Screw Loosening For Lumbar Fusion Surgery With Preoperative Volume Of Interest-Based Hounsfield Units in Lumbar Vertebral Bodies On Computed Tomography.
abstract: Study design Retrospective cohort study. Objective To assess whether preoperative Hounsfield unit (HU) values measured using the volume of interest (VOI) method on computed tomography (CT) scans predict pedicle screw loosening after single-level lumbar fusion surgery. Summary of background data Pedicle screw loosening is a major complication after spinal fusion surgery, particularly in patients with osteoporosis. While CT-derived HU values using region of interest (ROI) analysis have been associated with bone quality, the 3-dimensional VOI method enables volumetric assessment of the vertebral body. However, the clinical utility of VOI-based HU values for predicting screw loosening remains unclear. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 82 patients who underwent single-level lumbar interbody fusion with bilateral pedicle screw fixation. HU values at L1-L5 were measured using a 3D VOI technique. Screw loosening was assessed using follow-up CT scans taken at least 12 months after surgery. Differences in HU values between the loosening and nonloosening groups were evaluated. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to determine cutoff HU values and predictive performance. Results Pedicle screw loosening was observed in 26 out of 82 patients (31.7%). HU values were significantly lower in the loosening group across all vertebral levels (P<0.05). The mean HU value across L1-L5 was 235.7±35.2 HU in the loosening group and 283.2±65.6 HU in the nonloosening group (P<0.001). The average HU value across L1-L5 showed moderate predictive performance for screw loosening, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.723, a sensitivity of 88.5%, and a specificity of 50.0%. Conclusions Preoperative VOI-based HU values were significantly associated with pedicle screw loosening after single-level lumbar fusion surgery and demonstrated moderate predictive performance. VOI-based HU assessment may serve as a potential adjunctive tool for preoperative risk stratification of pedicle screw loosening.

title: Malposition Rates of Subaxial Cervical Pedicle Screws Placed Using Intraoperative Computed Tomography (O-arm)-Based Three-dimensional Navigation.
abstract: Study design Cohort retrospective review. Objective To investigate placement accuracy and malposition rates of cervical pedicle screws (CPS) using intraoperative CT (O-arm) based three-dimensional navigation. Background CPS placement is technically demanding due to small pedicle sizes and risk of damage to neurovascular structures in the neck. Computer navigation (CN) has been shown to improve accuracy rates in thoracolumbar pedicle screw placement. However, there are limited studies on CN use for placing CPS. Materials and methods We identified 100 patients who underwent CN CPS placement (C3-C7). Screw position was evaluated on axial, coronal, and sagittal planes and graded as follows: 0-fully in bone; I-minor breach deemed inconsequential (<25% of screw width); II-minor breach considered not ideal, but acceptable (25%-50% of screw width); and III-major breach considered dangerous or that compromised strength of fixation. Results Four hundred thirteen CN CPS screws (C3-C7) were placed in 100 patients (54M:46F). Rates of serious screw malpositions: combined Gr II/III = 42/413 (10.2%). Breaking down the combined Gr II/III screws per level: C3 = 8/33 (24.2%), C4 = 9/63 (14.3%), C5 = 8/72 (11.1%), C6 = 10/85 (11.8%), C7 = 7/160 (4.4%). Conclusion Our study shows a 10.2% nonoptimal rate (combined Gr II and III) using intraoperative three-dimensional imaging and CN. Our results add to a limited number of studies that have reported on this procedure. To our knowledge, this is the biggest study on a uniform technique of navigated pedicle screw placement that included only subaxial levels C3-C7.

title: The Radiographic Lung Edema Score in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Failure: Associations With Systemic Inflammatory Biomarkers and Multiple Organ Dysfunction.
abstract: Objectives Although chest radiographs (CXR) are among the most used imaging modalities in critically ill patients, their interpretation and clinical significance remain incompletely leveraged. The Radiographic Lung Edema (RALE) score is a prognostic bedside tool widely applied in adults to quantify lung edema on CXR. However, this score has been infrequently studied in children, and its potential to reflect broader aspects of critical illness pathophysiology beyond the lungs is unknown. We sought to determine the reproducibility of the RALE score, and whether higher RALE scores were associated with circulating inflammatory and endothelial biomarkers, multi-organ dysfunction, and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric acute respiratory failure (ARF). Design Retrospective cohort study. Setting Multicenter PICUs. Patients Critically ill children (2 wk to 17 yr old) receiving invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for ARF, enrolled in the CAF-PINT (Coagulation and Fibrinolysis in Pediatric Insulin Titration) study (2012-2016). Interventions None. Measurements and main results A baseline RALE score was calculated for each patient from a single CXR obtained within 72 hours of IMV initiation. Among 212 patients, RALE scores demonstrated good inter-rater reliability (intra-class coefficient 0.85; 95% CI, 0.82-0.87). After adjustment for ARF etiology and illness severity, higher RALE scores were associated with fewer 28-day ventilator-free days (sub-distribution hazard ratio per 1-sd increase, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Structural equation modeling demonstrated that this association was mediated through both pulmonary dysfunction, measured by the oxygenation index (β -0.14; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.22 to -0.06), and extrapulmonary organ dysfunction, measured by the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction score (β -0.05; 95% bootstrapped CI, -0.10 to -0.002). Similar associations were observed for 28-day PICU-free days. Finally, penalized regression selected soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and tumor necrosis factor receptor-1 as biomarkers associated with higher RALE scores. Conclusions We provide evidence that the RALE score is not solely a lung injury marker but also reflects broader systemic pathophysiology. These findings have important implications for the interpretation and clinical application of this bedside tool in pediatric ARF.

title: Expansion of the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score to Outpatients With Spine Metastases: Prospective Assessment on an Ongoing Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objectives For inpatients with spinal metastases, the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score accurately assesses prognosis, with scores of 0 to 3 exhibiting significantly longer survival than scores >3. This study examines the accuracy of this algorithm for outpatients prospectively considered for enrollment in the Spine Patient Optimal Radiosurgery Treatment for Symptomatic MEtastatic Neoplasms (SPORTSMEN) phase II randomized controlled trial. Methods From July 2025 to January 2026, outpatients at an NCI-designated cancer center were evaluated. Prognosis was assessed per an adjusted Metastatic Spine Score adjusted for consisting of: age at presentation (60+ vs. younger), duration of metastatic disease diagnosis (6+ mo vs. sooner), refractory to or on active systemic therapy (yes/no), additional nonspine metastatic focus (yes/no), severe malnutrition of chronic disease (yes/no), brain metastases (yes/no), and presenting symptomatology (asymptomatic or spine/back pain alone=no; additional neurological symptoms=yes) with each category scored a 0 (no) or 1 (yes) and a cumulative score derived. Scores of 0 to 3 were compared with scores >3 and correlated with outcomes. Positive prognosis=time to death/hospice >90 days from presentation. The Fisher test was used for statistical analysis. Results A positive prognosis was exhibited in 8/9 patients with scores of 0 to 3 (8/8 patients without brain metastases) versus 3/9 patients with scores >3 (P=0.0498). The overall accuracy of the Metastatic Spine Score (8/9 positive + 6/9 negative=14/18 patients) was 78%. Conclusion The Metastatic Spine Score provides an accurate prognostic assessment of outpatients with spine metastases, with scores of 0 to 3 yielding significantly better prognosis than scores >3. These findings also support brain MRI evaluation before radiotherapy decisions regarding spinal metastases. This study adds further support for establishing the Metastatic Spine Score as the standard-of-care for accurately evaluating prognosis in this patient population for outpatients as well as inpatients.

title: Racial, Ethnic, and Regional Influences on National Patterns of Mammographic Screening.
abstract: Objectives We sought to evaluate whether there were clinically significant disparities in screening mammography rates according to race, ethnicity, and United States geographic region in patients with access to health care systems. Methods We queried the Cosmos Epic national database to ascertain mammographic screening rates for women aged 50 to 65 who had 1 or more ambulatory encounters with a primary care physician between November 9, 2020, and November 8, 2023. Patients with a previous breast cancer and those with missing race or ethnicity data were excluded. Results The overall mammographic screening rate was 63.8% in the 7,837,164 individuals who met study criteria. There were no clinically meaningful differences in screening according to race. However, screening was less frequent in those with Hispanic ethnicity versus non-Hispanic (58.9% vs. 64.3%, P<0.001). Rates also varied according to region, with the lowest rates in the West (55.5%, P<0.001). Screening rates for Black and White groups were within 5% of one another in all 4 regions. With respect to ethnicity, the South was the only region where the Hispanic population rate had a lower rate over 5% (61.8% vs. 55.7%, P<0.001). Conclusions Many patients receiving health care in the US do not receive recommended mammogram screening, but there were no clinically significant differences by race. Lower rates were noted in Hispanic populations, particularly in the South. Targeted educational and community outreach efforts in this region are warranted.

title: What Are the Oncologic Outcomes of Patients With Osteosarcoma and Venous Tumor Thrombi Managed by an Aggressive Multidisciplinary Approach of Chemotherapy and Surgical Resection?
abstract: Background Macroscopic venous tumor thrombus (VTT) is a rare but aggressive manifestation of osteosarcoma that poses substantial challenges for both surgical management and systemic disease control. Our previous work characterized its frequency, radiographic features, and adverse prognostic association, particularly in pelvic osteosarcoma; however, surgical management was heterogeneous. The patient-level outcomes achieved after a standardized multidisciplinary treatment approach and the association between VTT resection strategy and postoperative oncologic outcomes remain unclear. Questions/purposes (1) What were the oncologic outcomes of patients with osteosarcoma with macroscopic VTT treated under a standardized treatment algorithm incorporating aggressive surgical resection? (2) Did the choice of VTT resection strategy affect oncologic outcomes? Methods We screened the records of 39 patients with treatment-naive osteosarcoma and macroscopic VTT identified on imaging who were treated according to a standardized multimodal treatment algorithm between 2019 and 2024. This algorithm consisted of standardized multimodal imaging at diagnosis to detect and characterize VTT. After biopsy confirmation, patients received four-agent neoadjuvant chemotherapy, preoperative inferior vena cava filter placement when technically feasible, and repeat imaging to reassess the resectability of both the primary tumor and VTT. Surgery was undertaken only when both lesions were considered resectable. VTT involving peripheral venous branches or completely occluded and enlarged major veins was managed with en bloc venous resection, whereas thrombectomy was performed for VTT involving patent or partially patent major veins. Postoperative chemotherapy was initiated 2 to 3 weeks after surgery. After excluding one patient without pathologic confirmation of the macroscopic VTT, two patients in whom en bloc resection of the primary tumor was not achieved, and seven patients who did not receive postoperative chemotherapy, 29 patients were included in this retrospective analysis. The study population was young (mean ± SD age 16 ± 7 years), with a slight male predominance (17 of 29 patients), and primary tumors were distributed between the extremities (16 of 29) and pelvis (13 of 29). More than half of the patients presented with metastatic disease (16 of 29), most VTTs involved major venous trunks (22 of 29), and 20 of 29 patients had < 90% tumor necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Given the high risk of early progression in these patients, progression-free survival (PFS) was selected as the primary endpoint. Secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), local recurrence-free survival (LRFS), and metastasis PFS (MPFS). Results Patients treated under the standardized algorithm had limited durable disease control, with disease progression in 26 of 29 patients, a median PFS of 7 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 0 to 16), and an estimated 2-year OS of 60%. Patients with localized disease had longer PFS (median 13 months [95% CI 8 to 19] versus 5 months [95% CI 4 to 5]; p = 0.046) and MPFS (median 13 months [95% CI 8 to 19] versus 4.6 months [95% CI 4 to 5]; p = 0.04) than those with metastatic disease. There were no differences in OS (not reached versus median 32 months [95% CI 10 to 54]; p = 0.52), PFS (median 11 months [95% CI 0 to 31] versus 6 months [95% CI 3 to 9]; p = 0.62), LRFS (median 21 months [95% CI 9 to 34] versus 61 months [95% CI 2 to 120]; p = 0.54), and MPFS (median 13 months [95% CI 0.3 to 25] versus 8 months [95% CI 3 to 13]; p = 0.24) between patients who had thrombectomy versus en bloc venous resection. Conclusion Despite a standardized multidisciplinary approach incorporating perioperative chemotherapy and aggressive resection of both the primary tumor and macroscopic VTT, progression remained frequent, and durable disease control was uncommon. Among these 29 selected patients, VTT resection strategy-thrombectomy versus en bloc venous resection-was not detectably associated with oncologic outcomes, although the two groups were not directly comparable. Surgeons should recognize that osteosarcoma with macroscopic VTT is a rare, highly aggressive condition for which current treatment modalities seldom achieve a cure and should carefully balance the potential oncologic benefit of aggressive surgery against its morbidity. Future prospective multicenter studies should refine patient-level selection criteria and directly evaluate the incorporation of adjuvant radiotherapy into this standardized treatment algorithm. Novel systemic therapies should also be investigated to improve control of metastatic and rapidly progressive disease. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic study.

title: How Much Do Horizontally Referenced and Interteardrop-referenced Acetabular Coverage Indices Differ During Standing in Adults With Hip Pain?
abstract: Background Acetabular coverage is conventionally assessed using the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and acetabular index. However, on standing radiographs, these measurements may be referenced either to the pelvis or to the weightbearing horizontal. Whether selection of these reference lines leads to clinically relevant differences in acetabular coverage interpretation is uncertain. Questions/purposes (1) How do horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements compare in patients with nonarthritic hip pain? (2) How are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity associated with differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced acetabular coverage measurements? (3) What are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity in young adults undergoing assessment for unilateral nonarthritic hip pain? (4) How are hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation associated with the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity? Methods In this retrospective comparative study, 598 patients evaluated at a tertiary-referral young-adult hip clinic between June 2021 and June 2025 were identified; 10% (60 of 598) were excluded for bilateral hip involvement or prior procedures, 5% (28 of 598) for insufficient radiographs, and 3% (17 of 598) for age 50 years or older, leaving 493 patients age 16 to 49 years with unilateral nonarthritic hip conditions and standing AP pelvic radiographs to be included. The mean ± SD age was 35 ± 8 years; 39% (191 of 493) were male. Diagnoses included dysplasia; cam-type, mixed, and pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement; isolated labral tears; and other nonarthritic hip conditions. In each hip, LCEA and acetabular index were measured using horizontal and interteardrop-referenced measurements, and classification disagreement was assessed using LCEA (< 20°, 20° to 25°, 25° to 40°, > 40°) and acetabular index (< 0°, 0° to 10°, > 10°) categories. Associations between pelvic obliquity magnitude and measurement-difference magnitude were assessed using linear regression, with directional relationships assessed graphically. Pelvic obliquity was measured as the angle between the interteardrop and horizontal reference lines, with direction defined relative to the clinically evaluated side. Hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation were compared across pelvic obliquity magnitude and direction groups. After interrater standardization, each patient was randomly allocated to one of two observers, who performed all measurements for that patient; a third observer reviewed a random sample. Interobserver intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.69 to 0.87. Results Mean ± SD absolute differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements were 2° ± 1° for both LCEA and acetabular index. Classification disagreement occurred in 14% (69 of 493) using LCEA-based categories and 10% (51 of 493) using acetabular index-based categories, most notably when interteardrop-referenced LCEA indicated borderline dysplasia and horizontally referenced LCEA indicated normal coverage (29% [28 of 95]). Each 1° increase in pelvic obliquity magnitude was associated with an approximately 1° greater measurement difference for LCEA (β = 0.89 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.86; p < 0.001) and acetabular index (β = 0.90 [95% CI 0.87 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.88; p < 0.001). Mean absolute pelvic obliquity magnitude was 2° ± 1°; 40% (197 of 493) had pelvic obliquity of 2° to < 5° and 3% (14 of 493) had pelvic obliquity ≥ 5°. The clinically evaluated hemipelvis was abducted in 44% (218 of 493), adducted in 39% (192 of 493), and neutral in 17% (83 of 493). Lesser trochanter-based hip-length discrepancy was 2 ± 2 mm with a neutral pelvis, 3 ± 3 mm with abduction, and 4 ± 3 mm with adduction (p < 0.001), and increased from 3 ± 3 mm to 5 ± 3 mm and 7 ± 3 mm across increasing pelvic obliquity magnitude categories (p < 0.001). Hip center of rotation-based values were 2 ± 2 mm in all three direction groups (p = 0.03) and 2 ± 2 mm, 3 ± 2 mm, and 3 ± 3 mm across increasing magnitude categories (p = 0.22). Conclusion These findings indicate that horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements can yield discordant acetabular coverage estimates and radiographic classifications for the same patient. As standing radiographs become more widely incorporated into hip evaluation, comparison of horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements may provide additional information by revealing pelvic-obliquity-associated differences in measured coverage while standing. In patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity, these differences may warrant consideration when interpreting acetabular morphology and discussing the relative indications for treatment or procedural options because they may lead clinicians to disagree about whether the same hip meets thresholds used in treatment planning. Future work should correlate measurements based on horizontal referencing and interteardrop referencing in patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity with clinical and surgical outcomes to (1) determine whether acetabular indices measured using the interteardrop line or floor-based horizontal reference confer superior clinical value and (2) define procedure-specific thresholds for relevant diagnostic subgroups. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: What Are the Long-term Outcomes of Periacetabular Osteotomy in a United States Cohort?
abstract: Background Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is an effective and common hip-preserving procedure used to treat symptomatic acetabular dysplasia of the hip. Evidence regarding long-term outcomes after PAO remains limited. Information regarding long-term outcomes may be important in developing reasonable expectations for both patients and surgeons to facilitate effective therapeutic decision-making. Questions/purposes (1) What is the likelihood of long-term hip preservation and the level of pain at a minimum of 25 years of follow-up after PAO? (2) What clinical and radiographic factors were associated with patients having a poor result, which we defined either as having THA or a WOMAC score of ≥ 10 points at the most recent survey? (3) What were the outcome scores of patients who underwent THA after PAO, and how did these scores compare to the scores of the preserved hips and to the scores of age-related norms? Methods We retrospectively evaluated the cohort of the first 142 patients (171 hips) who underwent PAO performed by one surgeon to treat symptomatic dysplasia between 1991 and 1998. Twenty-three percent (33 of 142) of patients (37 hips) were lost to follow-up. This included six patients (6 hips) who had died, 23 patients (26 hips) who could not be located, and four patients (5 hips) who did not complete questionnaires. Seventy-seven percent (109 of 142) of eligible patients (134 hips) returned complete questionnaires at a median (range) of 27 years (25 to 33) after PAO. Our analyzed group included 87% female patients (95 patients, 117 hips) and 13% male patients (14 patients, 17 hips). The median (range) age at surgery was 25 years (9 to 45). The median (range) time of review after PAO was 27 years (25 to 33). The 53 hips that had undergone THA were reviewed at a median (range) of 11 years (1 to 28) after the THA. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess survivorship free from conversion to THA. Hips were postoperatively evaluated using the pain subscale of the WOMAC index. title: Combination Therapy of Injectables With Energy-Based Treatments for Facial Rejuvenation: An Updated Review.
abstract: Background Fillers are frequently combined with other injectables and energy-based devices to target volume loss, dynamic rhytides, and photodamage. Questions remain regarding optimal treatment sequencing, safety, and synergistic clinical efficacy.OBJECTIVETo evalute the current evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of combining injectable therapies with energy-based treatments for facial rejuvenation. Methods MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched using keywords on dermal fillers with neuromodulators, intense pulsed light (IPL), laser, microfocused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V), high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), or radiofrequency (RF). Studies reporting safety, efficacy, sequencing, or clinical outcomes were included. Results Combining fillers with neuromodulators produces synergistic improvements in facial rejuvenation by addressing volume loss and muscular hyperactivity with superior outcomes and longer treatment durability compared with monotherapy. Intense pulsed light, nonablative lasers, MFU-V, HIFU, and RF appear safe when used with fillers, with studies demonstrating no significant adverse interactions or compromise of filler integrity. Combination treatment may enhance optimize facial contouring, improve skin quality, and improve patient satisfaction and retention. Histologic and clinical studies suggest synergistic effects when MFU-V/RF are combined with biostimulatory fillers. Conclusion Combination treatment with fillers and complementary modalities offers a comprehensive approach to facial rejuvenation. Current evidence supports the safety of most nonablative combination protocols. Additional studies are needed to assess the safety and efficacy of combining fillers with more aggressive resurfacing procedures and novel devices.

title: Intramuscular Well-differentiated Liposarcoma of the Brachioradialis Muscle.
abstract: Tumors of the brachioradialis muscle are rare, with only a few case reports including synovial sarcoma, fibrohistiocytoma and a benign lipoma. An intramuscular well-differentiated liposarcoma of the brachioradialis muscle is herein presented. A 44-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a slow-growing mass in the region of the brachioradialis muscle of the forearm, which did not directly involve any adjacent structures but was abutting the radial neurovascular bundle. The mass was bilobular with the larger portion being a benign lipoma with a deep component which was confirmed by immunohistochemistry to be a well-differentiated liposarcoma with no features of dedifferentiation. The tumor revealed spindle cells with retained expression of RB1, negative for desmin and CD34 and was fluorescence in situ hybridization positive with MDM2 amplification. The patient had a successful resection with clear margins and preservation of the radial neurovascular bundle that abutted the deep margin of the brachioradialis muscle. There was no neurovascular deficit or disability postoperatively. On 2-year follow-up after local radiotherapy the patient remains tumor free with no signs of recurrence or metastases on computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Well-differentiated intramuscular liposarcoma of the brachioradialis has not been documented based on our PubMed literature search. This case demonstrates a technique with preservation of forearm function coupled with recommendations for focused external beam radiotherapy. A multidisciplinary approach is essential, involving surgeons, pathologists, radiologists and oncologists. Accurate diagnosis relies on the integration of clinical, radiologic, and pathologic data, as well as thorough sampling of the tumor through excision biopsy.

title: Novel markers for atrial substrate characterization: implications on atrial fibrillation risk stratification.
abstract: Purpose of review Atrial fibrillation is increasingly recognized as a manifestation of an underlying atrial disease process that is incompletely captured by conventional temporal classification. This review examines established and emerging markers of atrial substrate and their potential role in atrial fibrillation risk stratification. Recent findings Electrocardiographic indices, left atrial volumetric and strain measures, computed tomography-derived left atrial wall characteristics, late gadolinium enhancement and flow assessment by cardiac magnetic resonance, high-density electroanatomic mapping, circulating biomarkers and genetic profiling provide complementary measures of electrical, structural, mechanical and hemodynamic remodelling. Recent studies have refined noninvasive identification of low-voltage substrate and risk stratification of atrial fibrillation progression and complications, evaluated substrate-guided ablation strategies, and expanded understanding of the prognostic significance of emerging substrate markers. Summary Multimodal atrial substrate characterization may improve prediction of atrial fibrillation onset and progression, thromboembolic complications and outcomes after rhythm-control therapy. Clinical translation requires standardized acquisition and analytical methods, reproducible thresholds, prospective validation of integrated risk models, and prospective trials demonstrating improved outcomes with substrate-guided management.

title: Advanced coronary computed tomography angiography plaque phenotyping for precision prevention.
abstract: Purpose of review In this review, we outline the role coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) plays in the diagnosis of coronary artery disease (CAD) and in facilitating risk assessment. Plaque quantification and phenotyping using CCTA is a promising approach in guiding cardiovascular preventive management. Recent findings There is growing interest in how artificial intelligence-based quantitative plaque analysis using CCTA (AI-CPA) can guide preventive therapy. The review summarizes studies that show prognostic utility of CCTA-derived plaque quantification and phenotyping as well as outlines more recent studies that show the impact of AI-CPA in patient management decisions, allowing a more individualized approach to preventive strategies. Summary CCTA provides a comprehensive assessment extending beyond coronary luminal stenosis to include plaque quantification, plaque phenotyping, functional assessment of stenotic lesions and vascular inflammation, further refining traditional approaches of risk prediction.In summary, the growing evidence highlights the importance of incorporating CCTA-based plaque volume and plaque phenotype analysis in better informing physicians about individual's risk and in guiding preventive management.

title: MRI-based biomarkers for risk stratification and assessment of treatment response in Metabolic dysfunction-associated Steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects up to 38% of the population globally. Liver biopsy, the historical reference standard, is invasive, subject to sampling error and not scalable. MRI-based biomarkers provide non-invasive, quantitative whole liver assessment. MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) is the most accurate noninvasive measure of steatosis (thresholds of 6.4%, 17.4% and 22.1% for grades ≥1, ≥2 and 3), and a ≥30% relative reduction is associated with histologic response. Liver stiffness by magnetic resonance elastography (MRE-LS) is the most accurate imaging biomarker for fibrosis: MRE-LS of 3.1-4.4 kPa corresponds to F2-F3 and ≥5 kPa to cirrhosis, and each 1-kPa increase is associated with a 43% higher risk of hepatic decompensation. Iron-corrected T1 is a sensitive but nonspecific marker of disease activity whose prognostic value requires further study. Composite scores, MAST, MEFIB, and MASH Resolution Index, combine imaging and blood tests for advanced fibrosis diagnosis and response assessment. MRE is cost-effective compared with vibration-controlled transient elastography for detecting advanced fibrosis. Artificial intelligence may broaden access by automating analysis and enabling PDFF from routine MRI. We review the evidence supporting these biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and regulatory use, and their role in clinical trials and in treatment decisions for approved MASH therapies.

title: Repeated Exposure to Military Low-Level Blast Is Associated With Regionally Specific Reductions in Gray Matter Volume in Breachers and Snipers.
abstract: Objective To examine the association between duration of repeated exposure to low-level blast and alteration in brain structure. Setting Data were collected at 2 neuroimaging facilities. Participants Canadian Armed Forces breachers ( n = 30) and snipers ( n = 31) with a history of repeated exposure to low-level blast (average years = 9.70, SD = 4.57) and sex- and age-matched active military controls ( n = 57). Design MRI and neurocognitive data from breachers and snipers were collected prospectively at baseline (time 1) and after a training exercise involving a concentrated regimen of blast exposure (time 2) (time gap = 80.56 days, SD = 36.90). Time 1 and time 2 data were used to assess the chronic and training-related effects of blast exposure, respectively. MRI and neurocognitive data from controls were collected twice with a comparable time gap. Main measures High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, plus neurocognitive measures. Results Voxel-based morphometry conducted on MRI data collected at time 1 demonstrated that compared with controls, there was lower regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers, and bilaterally in parahippocampal gyrus (bordering on amygdala) in breachers. Regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers predicted neurocognitive function. We did not observe any difference in regional white matter volume between groups at time 1, nor any changes in regional gray or white matter volume between time 1 and time 2. Conclusion Chronic but not training-related low-level blast exposure was associated with dissociable patterns of regional gray matter volume reduction in snipers and breachers, and regional gray matter volume predicted neurocognitive function in snipers. The differential pattern of structural alteration between breachers and snipers and its relationship with neurocognitive function in snipers can inform health monitoring programs for diagnosis and treatment of blast-exposed service members and Veterans.

title: Structure-Function Correlates of Radiation Chorioretinopathy: Insights from Microperimetry and Swept-Source OCTA.
abstract: Purpose To investigate optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) alterations and structure-function relationships in radiation chorioretinopathy (RCR) following external beam radiotherapy for choroidal melanoma. Methods Cross-sectional, case-control study including 21 eyes with RCR treated with CyberKnife (CK) or proton beam therapy (PBT), and 21 healthy fellow eyes as controls. Participants underwent swept-source 6×6-mm OCTA, spectral-domain OCT, and 68-stimulus mesopic microperimetry. OCTA metrics included vessel density (VD) of superficial (SCP) and deep capillary plexuses (DCP), foveal avascular zone (FAZ) area, and choriocapillaris flow-deficit percentage (CCFD%). Retinal thickness and functional outcomes-including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and mesopic retinal sensitivity (RS)-were analyzed within predefined regions. Generalized linear mixed-effects regression models assessed group differences and structure-function associations. Results Compared with controls, irradiated eyes demonstrated significantly reduced SCP and DCP VD, enlarged FAZ, and increased CCFD% across all macular regions (all p<0.001), despite preserved retinal thickness. Both BCVA and mesopic RS were significantly reduced in irradiated eyes (p<0.001), with no significant differences between CK- and PBT-treated eyes. In multivariable models, DCP VD within the 5-mm circle (p<0.01), CCFD% within the 3-5-mm ring (p<0.001), and parafoveal retinal thickness (p<0.05) were the strongest independent predictors of mesopic RS (adjusted R2=0.73). No biomarker was independently associated with BCVA (adjusted R2=0.44). Conclusions RCR is characterized by diffuse retinal and choriocapillaris microvascular impairment that correlates strongly with mesopic RS but not with BCVA. Microperimetry outperformed BCVA in detecting functional consequences of radiation-induced neurovascular damage, supporting the role of OCTA-derived metrics as relevant biomarkers for RCR diagnosis and monitoring.
