title: Primary Amenorrhea: Diagnostic Approach, Imaging Spectrum, and Common Pitfalls.
abstract: Primary amenorrhea is the absence of menarche in a 15-year-old adolescent girl who has developed secondary sex characteristics or a 13-year-old girl without development. Primary amenorrhea reflects disruption along the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian-uterine axis and may arise from a spectrum of anatomic, genetic, or functional abnormalities. Although primary amenorrhea is less common than secondary amenorrhea, recognition of the underlying level of dysfunction is essential for appropriate diagnosis and management as well as informed counseling regarding the patient's reproductive potential. A structured anatomic approach allows categorization of the causes into three levels based on the predominant site of dysfunction: level I, which involves the uterus and vaginal outflow tract; level II, which involves the ovaries and gonads; and level III, which involves the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. This classification system emphasizes a systematic and multidisciplinary approach to diagnosis and treatment, integrating clinical and biochemical testing and targeted imaging to localize the underlying dysfunction and guide treatment. Transabdominal US serves as the first-line imaging modality to help determine the presence and morphology of the pelvic organs. MRI provides detailed characterization of müllerian and urinary tract anomalies and allows evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary region when central causes are suspected.

title: Comprehensive Imaging Review of the Ureter.
abstract: The ureter is an important conduit between the kidney and the bladder and is frequently imaged to rule out cancer in the upper genitourinary tract. However, while malignancy can occur, a spectrum of other pathologic ureteral findings can exist, and these can be divided into congenital, intrinsic, and extrinsic abnormalities that range from postoperative and neoplastic conditions to inflammatory disease. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the ureter, including the ureteral anatomy, ureteral imaging strategies, and various ureteral conditions and their associated imaging features. It is important to identify congenital genitourinary variants, as these are frequently linked to further imaging recommendations, such as nuclear medicine renography and fluoroscopic voiding cystourethrography. Intrinsic abnormalities can be iatrogenic, infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic. Intrinsic ureteral strictures are most commonly iatrogenic, usually resulting from prior surgery or radiation therapy. Ureteral infections include tuberculosis, schistosomiasis, and Escherichia coli infection, which have varying imaging manifestations. Inflammatory conditions include ureteritis cystica and pseudodiverticulosis. Ureteral masses are rarely benign and are most commonly urothelial carcinomas. Processes in the abdomen and pelvis, including mass effect from pregnancy, ureteral compression from advanced pelvic floor prolapse, and rarely, ureteral obstruction from vaginal devices, also can affect the ureter. The ureter can be injured during pelvic surgery or trauma. It also may be involved by deep pelvic endometriosis, mass effect from extrinsic lesions, or reactive change from inflammatory processes. Radiologists need to have a clear understanding of the patient's history and the range of possible ureteral conditions to establish the optimal differential diagnosis.

title: Imaging in Systemic Sclerosis (Scleroderma).
abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) or scleroderma is a multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by a variable pattern of skin thickening and involvement of visceral organs. The pathophysiology is similar across all organs, which is chronic low-grade inflammation, with vasculopathy and eventual fibrosis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, particularly in patients with established disease comprising characteristic skin and visceral manifestations, with a supportive role of laboratory and imaging findings. The presence of radiologic signs such as hidebound bowel or a combination of patulous lower esophageal sphincter, pulmonary fibrosis, skin thickening, and Raynaud phenomenon is relatively specific for SSc. Nevertheless, imaging in SSc is primarily used to determine the pattern, severity, and complications of visceral organ involvement, rather than for diagnosis of SSc. Radiologic evaluation in SSc employs a wide gamut of investigations, depending on the organ of interest. For example, US is used for the skin and superficial tissues; fluoroscopy, CT, or MR enterography for the gastrointestinal tract; endoanal US or MRI for the internal anal sphincter; high-resolution CT for the lungs; echocardiography and cardiac MRI for SSc-related pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and cardiac disease; and radiography, CT, or MRI for musculoskeletal involvement. Early diagnosis of treatable features, such as PAH and gastroesophageal reflux, can help reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with SSc. Imaging is additionally useful to prognosticate and monitor the disease. The authors focus on the multisystem, multimodality imaging manifestations of SSc with relevant differential diagnoses to bridge the gaps in knowledge about SSc. © RSNA, 2026.

title: 3D and 4D Hysterosalpingo-Contrast Sonography: Advanced Tubal Patency Assessment.
abstract: Female infertility affects approximately 15% of couples of reproductive age, with tubal disease responsible for up to one-third of cases. Therefore, accurate, minimally invasive evaluation of tubal patency is a cornerstone of fertility assessment. Among the available modalities, including hysterosalpingography (HSG), MR HSG, and laparoscopic chromopertubation, hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography (HyCoSy) has gained prominence as a valuable alternative to conventional methods due to its safety, accessibility, and diagnostic reliability. Recent advances in contrast-enhanced US involving the use of second-generation microbubble agents combined with three-dimensional (3D) and four-dimensional (4D) acquisition technologies have significantly improved the performance of HyCoSy. These developments enable real-time volumetric visualization of the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes, enhancing both anatomic delineation and functional assessment of tubal patency. In addition, combined 3D and 4D (3D-4D) HyCoSy enables complementary evaluation of uterine morphology, adnexal structures, and associated infertility-related disorders such as endometriosis and adhesions, facilitating a comprehensive "one-stop" reproductive imaging approach. This article is intended to serve as a practical guide to performing 3D-4D HyCoSy with microbubble contrast agents, including preparation, technical parameters, and findings interpretation. In addition, the authors compare HyCoSy with conventional techniques, review characteristic imaging patterns of tubal patency and occlusion, and discuss potential pitfalls and preventive strategies. As an advanced US technology combined with a dynamic functional perspective, 3D-4D HyCoSy represents a powerful, cost-effective, and patient-friendly tool for integrated fertility evaluation in modern radiology practices.

title: 18 F-FET PET for Detection of Recurrent Disease in Gliomas: Tips and Tricks for Interpretation.
abstract: Gliomas are a heterogeneous group of primary brain tumors that are generally incurable. The current treatment paradigm for these tumors revolves around maximal safe resection and adjuvant chemoradiation; however, posttreatment changes can be difficult to distinguish from residual or recurrent disease. This makes it challenging to know whether treatments are working or the therapy should be escalated. Molecular imaging with amino acid PET has shown promise as a solution to this problem. The authors describe the interpretation considerations for the amino acid radiotracer fluorine 18-fluoroethyltyrosine (FET) in distinguishing posttreatment changes from recurrent glioma. The quantification of FET uptake on PET images and guidelines for interpretation are outlined.

title: Interpretable Artificial Intelligence for the Assessment of Mass Margin and Malignancy on Mammograms: A Reader Study.
abstract: Purpose To examine whether readers incorporate artificial intelligence explanations into their reasoning when assessing masses with mammography. Materials and Methods In an observer study, eight readers from April to August 2024 (four attending breast radiologists and four trainees) retrospectively interpreted 140 mammographic masses for malignancy. Readers were aided by a two-stage artificial intelligence system. The first stage classified mass margins, and the second estimated malignancy likelihood (0%-100%). Readers classified malignancy using two interfaces: a black-box interface providing only the malignancy score and an interpretable interface that also provided the margin assessment and a prototype-based explanation (based on a similar training mass). title: Management, Upgrade Rates, and Radiologic Surveillance of Screen-Detected High-Risk Breast Lesions.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the prevalence, upgrade rate, and radiologic surveillance management of high-risk lesions (HRLs) detected at screening mammography in a Dutch breast cancer screening population. Materials and Methods This retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database included patients recalled from the Dutch breast cancer screening program between January 2009 and July 2019. Incidence rates, diagnostic work-up, radiologic surveillance, and upgrades to (pre)malignancy after surgical excision and during radiologic surveillance were evaluated. Results Among 17 809 recalled patients, 514 patients with a mean age of 58 years ± 8.1 (SD) were diagnosed with an HRL. The incidence rate of HRLs was 0.83 per 1000 screens and 2.89 per 100 recalls. The majority of HRLs consisted of papillary lesions (34.4% [177 of 514]) and atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) (31.1% [160 of 514]). Surgical excision was performed in 233 cases (45.3%), resulting in 58 HRLs (24.9%) being upgraded to (pre)malignancy. Invasive tumors were mainly found in papillary lesions with atypia and ADH. Of patients diagnosed with an HRL, 324 (63.0%) had an indication for radiologic surveillance. Of these, 257 (79.3%) underwent surveillance, with 109 (42.4%) completing the recommended 5-year surveillance trajectory. During surveillance, 26 patients (10.1%) developed a (pre)malignancy. Invasive tumors were more frequently identified among HRLs upgraded during surveillance than among HRLs upgraded after surgical excision (17 of 26 [65%] vs 16 of 58 [28%]; P = .001). HRLs upgraded to invasive cancer were more likely to be triple-negative compared with screen-detected cancers (9.1% [3 of 33] vs 6.6% [215 of 3277]; P < .001). Conclusion Overall, 16.3% (84 of 514) of screen-detected HRLs were associated with a diagnosis of (pre)malignancy after surgical excision or during radiologic surveillance. Completion of the recommended 5-year surveillance trajectory was achieved in fewer than half of patients undergoing surveillance. Keywords: Breast Mammography, MR-Imaging, Ultrasound, Biopsy/Needle Aspiration, Screening Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Comparison of Two Deep Learning Models and Their Combination for 1-year Lung Cancer Detection in Two Screening Cohorts.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the performance of Sybil, a Medical Open Network for Artificial Intelligence (MONAI)-based nodule model, and their combination for 1-year lung cancer detection in two screening cohorts: the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and the Pamplona International Early Lung Cancer Action Program (P-IELCAP). Materials and Methods Baseline low-dose CT (LDCT) examinations from the NLST and the P-IELCAP were analyzed. A prespecified OR-stacked composite model combining Sybil, a MONAI-based nodule model, and a safety-net rule (MONAI-detected nodule > 6 mm with detection confidence > 0.95) was developed and evaluated for 1-year lung cancer detection. Model discrimination was assessed by using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and operating-point performance metrics were calculated. Results A total of 5110 baseline LDCT examinations were analyzed, including 2343 from NLST and 2767 from P-IELCAP, with 65 lung cancers diagnosed within 1 year. Mean age, mean pack-years, and percentage of female participants were 61.6 years ± 5.1 (SD), 57.3 pack-years ± 24.8, and 39.4% (923 of 2343), respectively, in NLST and 56.0 years ± 9.5, 34.4 pack-years ± 21.5, and 28.6% (791 of 2767), respectively, in P-IELCAP. Lung cancer incidence (per 1000 person-years) was higher in NLST than in P-IELCAP (17.7 vs 8.7; P = .006). Mean Sybil 1-year lung cancer probabilities (scaled by 1000 for presentation) were also higher in NLST than in P-IELCAP (16.4 vs 9.9; P < .01). Sybil achieved an AUC of 0.93 in both cohorts, whereas the MONAI-based model achieved AUCs of 0.90 in NLST and 0.79 in P-IELCAP. The composite model missed two of 65 1-year lung cancers while correctly classifying 2731 of 4965 (55.0%) noncancer examinations as negative, yielding a sensitivity of 63 of 65 (96.9%) and a positive predictive value of 63 of 2297 (2.7%). Conclusion For 1-year lung cancer detection with LDCT, the composite AI model achieved high sensitivity while maintaining acceptable specificity. Keywords: Applications-CT, Thorax, Pulmonary, Sybil, MONAI, NLST, P-IELCAP, Lung Cancer, Low Dose Computed Tomography Supplemental material is available for this article. © RSNA, 2026.

title: Presentation of Kaposi Sarcoma With Extensive Skin Lesions and Bone Involvement After Ten Years of Virally Suppressed HIV Infection and Restored CD4 Cell Counts.
abstract: Background Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an HHV-8-associated angioproliferative tumor that can occur in persons living with HIV despite effective antiretroviral therapy. Although cutaneous KS after immune restoration has been described, extensive osseous involvement after prolonged viral suppression remains uncommon. Case presentation A 51-year-old man with HIV-1 infection and sustained viral suppression for more than 10 years presented with severe pain in the right foot, progressive swelling of the legs, and skin discoloration. Initial diagnostic considerations included gout, stasis dermatitis, and osteomyelitis. Persistent symptoms despite treatment prompted further investigation. MRI demonstrated multiple pathological bone lesions in both feet. Skin and bone biopsies subsequently confirmed HHV-8-positive KS involving the skin and bone. At diagnosis, the patient had a CD4 cell count of 750 cells/μL and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 1.42, with an undetectable HIV viral load. Treatment with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin resulted in a substantial clinical and metabolic response, but the patient experienced two subsequent recurrences. Symptomatic localized osseous progression of KS in the left foot was treated with radiotherapy, resulting in significant pain relief, while pegylated liposomal doxorubicin was continued with a favorable clinical and metabolic response. Conclusion This case highlights that extensive cutaneous and osseous KS can develop and recur despite prolonged viral suppression and restoration of conventional markers of immune function. KS should therefore remain in the differential diagnosis of unexplained cutaneous lesions, edema, and bone lesions in persons living with HIV, even when CD4 cell counts are preserved and HIV viral load remains undetectable. Long-term clinical surveillance and individualized multimodal treatment may be required.

title: Pancolitis due to Tuberculosis Masquerading as Inflammatory Bowel Disease in a 43-Year-Old Woman: Diagnostic Challenges in a Resource-Limited Setting-A Case Study and Literature Review From Ethiopia.
abstract: Background Gastrointestinal tuberculosis (GI TB) predominantly affects the ileocecal region, making primary colonic involvement exceptionally rare. In TB-endemic, resource-limited settings, differentiating colonic TB from inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)-particularly Crohn's disease (CD)-presents a formidable diagnostic dilemma owing to overlapping clinical, radiological, and ileocolonoscopic features, often leading to diagnostic delays, misdiagnosis, and subsequent complications. Initial clinical presentation treatment and diagnostic re‐evaluation In May 2026, a 43-year-old Ethiopian woman presented to Jimma University Medical Center with a 10-month history of progressive colicky abdominal pain, chronic watery diarrhea, postprandial nonbilious vomiting, and significant weight loss. Prior empirical regimens of antihelminthic agents and broad-spectrum antibiotics administered at peripheral health facilities yielded no clinical improvement. Initial laboratory workup revealed microcytic hypochromic anemia (hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL), a significantly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (92 mm/h), hypoalbuminemia (2.8 g/dL), and a normal carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level (4 ng/mL). Ileocolonoscopy demonstrated superficial ulceration involving the ascending colon and hepatic flexure in a continuous form with numerous inflammatory polyps, and a small deep ulceration at the terminal ileum. Initial histopathology demonstrated chronic active inflammation without evidence of malignancy or granuloma formation. With a presumed diagnosis of CD, treatment was initiated with prednisolone and azathioprine, which might have contributed to the suspected deterioration of the clinical condition, warranting re-evaluation with contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis, which demonstrated diffuse, long-segment circumferential wall thickening involving the terminal ileum, the entire colon, and the rectum, alongside pericolic fat stranding, a mesenteric phlegmon, and multiple necrotic mesenteric lymph nodes, with the largest measuring 2 × 3 cm with peripheral rim enhancement. Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the necrotic lymph nodes revealed epithelioid granulomas and characteristic caseous necrosis. With the above evidence, terminal ileitis and pancolitis due to TB were considered, immunosuppressive medications were discontinued, and standard antituberculosis therapy (2RHZE/4RH) was promptly initiated. The patient started to experience clinical improvement, achieving full resolution of her constitutional and abdominal symptoms and gaining weight at 1 month of follow-up. Conclusion Diagnosing GI TB-especially in atypical sites such as the colon-presents a critical challenge in resource-limited, TB-endemic settings, where differentiating it from IBDs, especially CD, is vital to prevent severe complications from inappropriate therapy. To avoid misdiagnosing GI TB as IBD (which risks disseminated infection from immunosuppression) or IBD as TB (which worsens bowel stricture, fistulae, and perforation), clinicians must perform mandatory pretreatment TB screening using radiologic, immunologic, molecular, and culture modalities before initiating immunosuppressive agents. Furthermore, diagnostic accuracy requires obtaining deep submucosal biopsies during ileocolonoscopy to detect characteristic granulomatous lesions if present. Finally, when an empirical anti-TB trial is necessary, it must be strictly time-limited and followed by objective re-evaluation at 8 weeks-including repeat endoscopy and biopsy-rather than relying solely on clinical symptomatic improvement.

title: Primary Pericardial Synovial Sarcoma Presenting as a Giant Intrapericardial Mass: A Case Report.
abstract: Primary pericardial synovial sarcoma is an extremely rare malignant tumor with nonspecific presentation and poor prognosis. We report the case of a 29-year-old woman whose pericardial mass was detected during a workplace health examination. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a giant intrapericardial mass predominantly compressing the left atrium. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a heterogeneous intrapericardial mass extending from the left margin of the main pulmonary artery to the left atrioventricular groove, with partial invasion of the left atrial cavity. Ultrasound-guided biopsy showed a monophasic spindle-cell neoplasm. Immunohistochemistry showed focal weak positivity for pancytokeratin and epithelial membrane antigen, positivity for vimentin and D2-40, weak positivity for CD99, and a Ki-67 labeling index of approximately 15%. Fluorescence in situ hybridization using an SS18 break-apart probe demonstrated split red and green signals in tumor-cell nuclei, consistent with SS18 rearrangement. The patient declined surgical resection and adjuvant therapy and died 22 months after diagnosis. This case emphasizes that multimodality imaging is essential for defining tumor extent but cannot establish histological subtype. Integrated histology, immunohistochemistry, and SS18 fluorescence in situ hybridization are required for diagnostic confirmation.

title: Necrotic Immature Permanent Incisors: Apexification With Calcium Hydroxide and MTA Versus Pulp Revascularization: A Case Report With Long-Term Follow-Up.
abstract: Pulp necrosis in immature permanent teeth interrupts root development and prevents physiological apical closure, making endodontic management particularly challenging. Apexification with calcium hydroxide or mineral trioxide aggregate (MTA) has long been considered the standard treatment for these teeth by promoting the formation of an apical barrier and achieving periapical healing. However, neither approach allows continued root maturation, leaving thin dentinal walls that may compromise the long-term prognosis. Regenerative endodontic treatment, including pulp revascularization, has emerged as a biologically based alternative capable of promoting continued root development and reinforcing root structure. This report presents two clinical cases of necrotic immature permanent incisors managed at the Department of Pediatric Dentistry, CCTD Casablanca, Morocco, illustrating calcium hydroxide apexification, MTA apexification, and pulp revascularization. Both treatment approaches resulted in satisfactory clinical and radiographic healing. However, pulp revascularization demonstrated the additional benefit of continued root maturation, whereas apexification provided apical closure without further root development. These cases highlight the indications, advantages, limitations, and clinical outcomes of each therapeutic approach and support the current evidence favoring regenerative endodontic treatment whenever clinical conditions are suitable.

title: Conservative Management of a Cervical Horizontal Root Fracture in a Mature Permanent Incisor: A Case Report.
abstract: Cervical root fractures in permanent teeth are uncommon traumatic injuries that may present significant therapeutic challenges and are associated with a poor prognosis. This report describes the conservative management of a cervical horizontal root fracture in a permanent maxillary central incisor in a healthy 13-year-old girl who presented 48 hours after a sports-related trauma. Clinical examination revealed displacement and increased mobility of Tooth 21 and gingival bleeding. Periapical radiography showed a complete horizontal root fracture in the cervical third, at the level of the alveolar crest, with approximately 2 mm displacement between the fragments. The coronal fragment was repositioned and stabilized with a flexible splint fabricated from monofilament nylon fishing line and composite resin. A removable protective appliance was also provided during the initial 4 weeks to prevent premature contact and improve comfort. Considering the unfavorable prognostic factors, splinting was maintained for 7 months. At that time, localized gingival inflammation was observed around the splint, and the splint was removed. The gingival condition resolved within 1 week. Follow-up continued, and a mouthguard was subsequently provided for use during sports activities. At the 12-month follow-up, the tooth remained asymptomatic and functional, with maintained pulp sensibility and findings compatible with favorable healing. The natural tooth was preserved.

title: Two Cases of Lung Nodules Presenting With Kappa Light Chain Deposition Disease/Congo-Red Negative AL Amyloidosis.
abstract: Light Chain Deposition Disease (LCDD) is a rare disorder characterized by the extracellular accumulation of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains in various organs, most commonly the kidneys, but occasionally the heart, liver, and lungs. Pulmonary LCDD (PLCDD) is an exceedingly rare manifestation that can closely resemble other pulmonary diseases both radiologically and histologically. Unlike amyloidosis, LCDD does not exhibit Congo red positivity or apple-green birefringence under polarized light, which can complicate diagnosis. Mass spectrometry (MS) has emerged as a valuable diagnostic tool in such cases, providing definitive identification of monoclonal light chains when traditional histopathological techniques are inconclusive. We present two cases of pulmonary nodular LCDD, both in women with autoimmune backgrounds, including Sjögren's syndrome. Both patients presented with pulmonary nodules demonstrating FDG uptake on PET-CT scans. Histologic examination revealed amorphous eosinophilic deposits without Congo red birefringence. Proteomic analysis via laser microdissection and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) confirmed the presence of kappa light chain deposits, supporting a diagnosis of LCDD or non-Congophilic AL-type amyloidosis. One patient had no evidence of systemic disease, whereas the other showed clonal plasma cell infiltration with kappa light chain restriction, suggestive of a low-grade B-cell neoplasm. These cases underscore the diagnostic complexity of PLCDD and highlight the critical role of MS in differentiating it from pulmonary classical amyloidosis. Nodular PLCDD may follow an indolent course and often lacks systemic involvement, whereas diffuse forms carry a poorer prognosis because of extensive pulmonary and systemic involvement. Treatment remains focused on managing the underlying plasma cell disorder, though standardized therapeutic protocols are lacking because of the rarity of the condition. Our findings emphasize the need for increased clinical awareness and advanced diagnostic strategies to appropriately identify and manage PLCDD.

title: Uniportal Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery for Intrathoracic Phrenic Nerve Schwannomas: A Report of 2 Cases and Literature Review.
abstract: Phrenic nerve schwannoma (PNS) is an extremely rare benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor with atypical clinical manifestations, leading to frequent preoperative misdiagnosis. This study aimed to explore the clinical efficacy and surgical strategy of uniportal video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (uni-VATS) for intrathoracic PNS. Two asymptomatic patients with intrathoracic PNS admitted to our hospital were enrolled, including one 55-year-old male with a left anterior mediastinal mass and one 22-year-old female with a right middle mediastinal mass. Preoperative contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated well-circumscribed cystic-solid mediastinal masses with heterogeneous enhancement. Both patients received uni-VATS treatment: end-to-end phrenic nerve anastomosis was performed after tumor resection for the first case due to dense tumor-nerve adhesion, while intracapsular enucleation was adopted for the second case with clear dissection planes. The operative time was 69 and 60 min, intraoperative blood loss was 10 mL in both cases, and postoperative hospital stay was 3 days for both patients without perioperative complications. Postoperative histopathology and immunohistochemistry confirmed benign schwannoma with positive S-100 and SOX10 expression. During follow-up, only mild asymptomatic left diaphragmatic elevation was observed in the first case, and no tumor recurrence or nerve dysfunction occurred in either case. Uni-VATS is a safe and minimally invasive approach for localized intrathoracic PNS. Individualized surgical strategies based on tumor-nerve anatomical characteristics can maximize phrenic nerve function preservation and achieve favorable long-term prognosis.

title: Challenges in the Management of Giant Strangulated Hiatal Hernia: A Case Report.
abstract: A giant hiatal hernia (GHH) is generally defined as the herniation of more than half of the stomach into the thoracic cavity, although definitions vary in the literature, with some authors considering herniation of more than one-third of the stomach sufficient for diagnosis. Strangulation is a rare but life-threatening complication that may lead to vascular compromise, gastric ischemia, and ultimately necrosis, requiring urgent diagnosis and individualized surgical management. We report the case of a 54-year-old man with long-standing gastroesophageal reflux disease who presented with chest pain and recurrent vomiting. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a giant type III hiatal hernia with approximately two-thirds of the stomach herniated into the thoracic cavity and associated gastric obstruction. Emergency laparoscopy revealed a severely twisted stomach with extensive necrosis of the fundus and greater curvature. Given the size of the hernia, an adequate exposure of the hiatal area was difficult to achieve, necessitating conversion to a left subcostal laparotomy. After dissection of the two diaphragmatic crus, the sac was reduced and excised, allowing complete reduction of the stomach back into the abdominal cavity. The necrotic areas were managed by longitudinal atypical gastrectomy. Given the large hiatal defect, anterior cruroplasty was performed to prevent an excessive angulation of the esophagus. No antireflux system could be implemented as the fundus was fully removed and Staple-line integrity was confirmed by an intraoperative methylene blue leak test. The postoperative course was uneventful with minimal residual reflux, treated by proton pump inhibitor therapy. We provide this case to demonstrate the treatment of a giant strangulated hernia and challenges stemming from the alternative surgical approach in laparoscopic and robot-assisted practice.

title: Haemorrhage Into an Arachnoid Cyst With Bilateral Subdural Haematoma Without the Apparent History of Trauma: A Rare Case Report of a Rare Entity in Young Adult.
abstract: Arachnoid cysts (ACs) are benign cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-filled lesions that are usually identified incidentally and remain asymptomatic. Haemorrhagic complications are uncommon and are typically associated with trauma, whereas haemorrhage into an AC with associated subdural haematoma (SDH) without the apparent history of trauma is exceedingly rare. We report the case of a 25-year-old immunocompetent male who presented with acute headache and vomiting without any preceding trauma. Neurological examination was normal, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15/15, and had no deficits. Neuroimaging demonstrated SDH involving left frontoparietotemporal and right parietal region with haemorrhage into an underlying arachnoid cyst. Magnetic resonance imaging was essential in confirming the diagnosis and delineating the associated pathology. The patient underwent elective left pterional craniotomy with evacuation of the haematoma and marsupialisation of the cyst. Postoperatively, he recovered completely without neurological deficits and remained asymptomatic at one-year follow-up. Haemorrhage into an arachnoid cyst without history of trauma is a rare but important differential diagnosis in young patients presenting with acute headache in the absence of trauma. Because clinical presentation may mimic other acute intracranial pathologies, early recognition and timely surgical intervention are crucial for achieving favourable neurological and long-term outcomes.

title: Cyst of the Canal of Nuck in an Adult Woman: Diagnostic Workup and Surgical Management-A Case Report.
abstract: Cysts of the canal of Nuck are rare congenital abnormalities resulting from incomplete obliteration of the processus vaginalis in females and may mimic more common causes of inguinal swelling, particularly inguinal hernia. We report the case of a 35-year-old woman presenting with a symptomatic right inguinal swelling. Ultrasonography demonstrated a well-defined avascular cystic lesion, and, in this case, contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) was used for further anatomical characterization, showing a thin-walled fluid-filled structure extending along the right inguinal canal without bowel herniation or radiological communication with the peritoneal cavity. A cyst of the canal of Nuck was therefore suspected preoperatively. The patient underwent complete surgical excision through an open inguinal approach, without mesh repair. Histopathological examination confirmed a benign mesothelial-lined cyst consistent with a cyst of the canal of Nuck. At 1-month follow-up, the patient was completely asymptomatic, with no clinical or ultrasonographic evidence of recurrence. This case emphasizes the importance of including this uncommon entity in the differential diagnosis of female inguinal masses and illustrates how first-line ultrasonography, with selective cross-sectional imaging when additional anatomical definition is required, can support individualized surgical planning.

title: Extensive Dural Metastasis as Initial Presentation of Metastatic Prostate Cancer: A Case Report With Durable Disease Control Following Multimodal Treatment.
abstract: Central nervous system involvement in prostate cancer is rare, particularly in the form of dural or pachymeningeal metastases. We report the case of a 72-year-old man presenting with visual disturbances without hemianopsia, and right-sided headache since several weeks caused by an extensive right temporal dural-based lesion with intracranial extension. A minimally invasive frontotemporal burr-hole biopsy was performed for histopathological clarification. Histological and immunohistochemical analyses confirmed metastatic prostatic adenocarcinoma with expression of cytokeratin 8, NKX3.1, PSA, and PSMA. Subsequent systemic staging demonstrated metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer with pulmonary, lymphatic, and extensive osseous metastases. The patient underwent focal radiotherapy (36 Gy in 12 fractions) to the dural lesion and systemic treatment with androgen deprivation therapy and enzalutamide. Due to dizziness and sweating, enzalutamide dosage was reduced from 160 to 80 mg/day with maintained therapeutic response. At approximately 15 months of follow-up, the patient remained neurologically stable with durable local disease control on cranial MRI, marked biochemical response (PSA decline from 177 to 0.6 ng/mL), and no evidence of systemic progression. This case highlights the importance of considering metastatic prostate cancer in the differential diagnosis of dural-based intracranial lesions in elderly men and demonstrates that individualized multimodal treatment can achieve durable disease control even in rare metastatic presentations.

title: NanoScope-Assisted Arthroscopic Repair of a Full-Thickness Supraspinatus Tear With Concomitant Shoulder Pathology: A Case Report.
abstract: Case A 62-year-old right-hand-dominant woman presented with progressive atraumatic left shoulder pain, weakness, and limited range-of-motion (ROM) refractory to conservative management. Examination revealed weakness of the supraspinatus and positive impingement signs. MRI demonstrated a medially retracted full-thickness supraspinatus tear with subacromial bursitis and acromioclavicular arthrosis. Intraoperative assessment identified a partial tear of the biceps tendon at the superior labral insertion, a degenerative Type-II superior labrum anterior-to-posterior (SLAP) lesion, posterior-superior labral tearing without complete detachment, and glenoid chondromalacia. She underwent NanoScope-assisted arthroscopic double-row supraspinatus repair with biceps tenotomy, labral debridement, glenoid chondroplasty, subacromial decompression, acromioplasty, and distal claviculectomy. At 6 weeks, ultrasound (US) demonstrated an intact-appearing supraspinatus repair without retraction. At 1-year telehealth follow-up, the patient reported favorable patient-reported outcomes, including an American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score of 88/100, shoulder surgery questionnaire 8 score of 92.5/100, single assessment numeric evaluation (SANE) scores of 95% for the left shoulder and 90% for the right shoulder, and visual analog scale (VAS) pain score of 0/10. Conclusion This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of NanoScope-assisted arthroscopic repair of a full-thickness supraspinatus tear with concomitant shoulder pathology.

title: Post-Traumatic Abdominal Aortic Dissection Associating Solid Organ Injury in a Child.
abstract: Introduction Handlebar injuries are frequent events in children, often perceived as minor, but may result in severe intra-abdominal damage. Case presentation We report the case of a 13-year-old boy who sustained a blunt abdominal trauma following impact against a bicycle handlebar. In this case, the trauma produced an unusual and potentially life-threatening combination of lesions, including massive hemoperitoneum, a deep hepatic laceration, a severe pancreatic injury with disruption of the main pancreatic duct, and a post-traumatic dissection of the infrarenal abdominal aorta. Results The patient was admitted in critical condition and underwent prompt clinical, laboratory, and radiological evaluation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed the extent of the abdominal injuries and confirmed the vascular involvement. Given the complexity and severity of the findings, management required a rapid multidisciplinary approach involving pediatric surgeons, interventional radiologists, vascular surgeons, and gastroenterologists. The infrarenal aortic dissection was treated urgently with an endovascular approach using the placement of a covered stent, allowing successful exclusion of the lesion and stabilization of the vascular injury while avoiding open surgery. The hepatic injury was managed conservatively with close hemodynamic and radiological monitoring. During the subsequent clinical course, the patient developed a large post-traumatic pancreatic pseudocyst related to the pancreatic duct disruption. This complication was successfully treated with endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage using a lumen-apposing metal stent (LAMS), which allowed effective internal drainage and progressive resolution of the collection. Conclusions This case highlights the potentially severe nature of bicycle handlebar injuries in children and emphasizes the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for occult intra-abdominal and vascular injuries. Early diagnosis and timely multimodal management are crucial to optimize outcomes in these complex traumatic scenarios.

originalAbstract:
Introduction

Handlebar injuries are frequent events in children, often perceived as minor, but may result in severe intra-abdominal damage.

Case presentation

We report the case of a 13-year-old boy who sustained a blunt abdominal trauma following impact against a bicycle handlebar. In this case, the trauma produced an unusual and potentially life-threatening combination of lesions, including massive hemoperitoneum, a deep hepatic laceration, a severe pancreatic injury with disruption of the main pancreatic duct, and a post-traumatic dissection of the infrarenal abdominal aorta.

Results

The patient was admitted in critical condition and underwent prompt clinical, laboratory, and radiological evaluation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed the extent of the abdominal injuries and confirmed the vascular involvement. Given the complexity and severity of the findings, management required a rapid multidisciplinary approach involving pediatric surgeons, interventional radiologists, vascular surgeons, and gastroenterologists. The infrarenal aortic dissection was treated urgently with an endovascular approach using the placement of a covered stent, allowing successful exclusion of the lesion and stabilization of the vascular injury while avoiding open surgery. The hepatic injury was managed conservatively with close hemodynamic and radiological monitoring. During the subsequent clinical course, the patient developed a large post-traumatic pancreatic pseudocyst related to the pancreatic duct disruption. This complication was successfully treated with endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage using a lumen-apposing metal stent (LAMS), which allowed effective internal drainage and progressive resolution of the collection.

Conclusions

This case highlights the potentially severe nature of bicycle handlebar injuries in children and emphasizes the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for occult intra-abdominal and vascular injuries. Early diagnosis and timely multimodal management are crucial to optimize outcomes in these complex traumatic scenarios.

title: Late Presentation of Fetus in Fetu in a 10-Year-Old Boy.
abstract: Fetus in fetu (FIF) is a rare congenital anomaly in which a dysmorphic, parasitic twin is retained within the body of its host twin. It typically presents in infancy, shows a slight male predominance, and is most often located in the retroperitoneum. Differentiating FIF from an abdominal teratoma on imaging is important, as the two entities can closely resemble one another. We report the case of a 10-year-old boy who presented with abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and unintentional weight loss. Antenatal history was unremarkable. Abdominal examination revealed mild distension and left-sided tenderness. Ultrasonography demonstrated an 8.5 × 10.4 × 11.1 cm mass-like lesion in the left hypochondrium, and a provisional diagnosis of teratoma versus FIF was considered. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen showed a large, well-defined, heterogeneous mesenteric mass measuring 10.0 × 11.0 × 14.0 cm containing macroscopic fat, dense tooth-like calcifications, and osseous elements with attenuation of up to 1450 Hounsfield units, together with a well-formed fetal skeleton. Serum tumor markers were within normal limits. A presumptive diagnosis of FIF, supported by imaging and by intraoperative findings that satisfied the Willis criteria, was made at exploratory laparotomy; histopathological confirmation could not be obtained because the specimen was inadequately fixed prior to processing, so a highly differentiated fetiform teratoma cannot be entirely excluded. The child remained well at last follow-up, about 10 weeks after discharge; longer surveillance is required. This case illustrates that FIF, although classically a diagnosis of infancy, should remain in the differential diagnosis of a complex abdominal mass in an older child, and highlights the role of the Willis criteria, radiological correlation, and intraoperative findings when histopathology is unavailable.

title: Explainable Hybrid Deep-Radiomic Graph Learning Framework for Automated IDC Aggressiveness Grading From Whole-Slide Histopathology Images.
abstract: Breast cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide. Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a crucial role in the diagnosis and grading of breast cancer subtypes. Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) is the most prevalent and heterogeneous subtype of breast cancer, and its aggressiveness grading has important prognostic value. Manual grading of IDC aggressiveness using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained WSIs is tedious and subjective. In this study, we address the issues of automated IDC aggressiveness grading using an explainable hybrid deep-radiomic graph learning framework. The proposed pipeline jointly performs tumor segmentation, feature representation, and classification within an end-to-end framework. The tumor is segmented using an attention U-Net followed by dense conditional random field (DenseCRF) segmentation refinement. Deep convolutional features and radiomic features encoding texture, morphology, and intensity statistics are extracted from the segmented tumor region and combined to form hybrid deep-radiomic features. Spatial graphs constructed from these hybrid features are subsequently processed using a graph attention network (GAT)-based graph neural network (GNN) with attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) to reason about the relationships between different patches for slide-level grade prediction. Extensive experiments performed on two datasets, BreakHis and BACH, show that our proposed architecture demonstrates improved performance in IDC aggressiveness grading when compared with convolutional neural network (CNN) and GNN baselines with an accuracy of 98.3%, macro-F1 score of 0.968, ROC-AUC score of 0.98, and Dice score of 0.932. The explainability of proposed model with Grad-CAM visual explanations, graph attention scores, and SHAP-based feature importance scores for individual radiomic features are presented.

title: Association Between Pulmonary Artery Diameter on CT and Clinical Outcomes in COVID-19: A 1000-Patient Retrospective Analysis.
abstract: Background We evaluated the association between main pulmonary artery (PA) diameter on chest CT and CT-defined lung involvement, intensive care unit (ICU) hospitalization, and in-hospital mortality in patients hospitalized with COVID-19. Methods This retrospective cohort included 1000 adults with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 treated at Namazi and Shahid Faghihi Hospitals in 2020. For each patient, the first routine noncontrast chest CT obtained after admission was analyzed, provided it had been performed within the first 72 h. Main PA diameter was measured manually on axial images proximal to the PA bifurcation. Associations with age, sex, CT severity, ICU hospitalization, and in-hospital outcome were evaluated. Results The mean age was 56 ± 17.7 years; 525 patients (52.5%) were men and 475 (47.5%) were women. Mean PA diameter was 27.07 ± 3.84 mm. Men had a larger mean PA diameter than women (27.40 ± 3.77 vs. 26.69 ± 3.88 mm; p = 0.004), and age showed a weak positive correlation with PA diameter ( r = 0.282, p < 0.001). PA diameter increased across CT severity categories and was greater among patients who died and among those hospitalized in the ICU (all p < 0.001). Conclusions Larger PA diameter was associated with greater CT-defined lung involvement, ICU hospitalization, and in-hospital mortality. Because the analyses were unadjusted and observational, these findings do not establish independent or incremental prognostic value.

title: Morphological, Morphometric, Radiographic, and Computed Tomographic Study of the Cervical Vertebrae in the Persian Squirrel (Sciurus anomalus).
abstract: Background Accurate knowledge of cervical spine morphology in arboreal rodents is crucial for understanding baseline anatomical structure and assisting in clinical diagnostic evaluations. This study investigated the descriptive anatomy, morphometry, and radiographic/computed tomographic (CT) features of the cervical vertebrae in the Persian squirrel ( Sciurus anomalus ). Materials and methods Four healthy adult male Persian squirrels underwent digital radiography and multislice CT scanning, and four separate dry skeletons were evaluated for osteological investigations. Morphometric parameters were measured in triplicate. Data normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Variations across the cervical series (C2-C7) were evaluated separately for CT and caliper datasets using repeated-measures ANOVA (RM-ANOVA) with the Bonferroni adjustment ( p < 0.05). Results The cervical vertebral formula was seven (C7). Straight and curvilinear cervical spine lengths were 23.15 ± 0.3 mm and 28.34 ± 0.4 mm, respectively. The atlas vertebra (C1) lacked a true vertebral body, with a ventral arch length (VAL) of 3.12 ± 0.18 mm on CT. The axis vertebra (C2) exhibited the maximum vertebral body length (VBL: 6.29 ± 0.18 mm on CT). Middle cervical vertebrae (C3-C5) displayed smaller, relatively uniform linear dimensions and lacked a ventral crest. In the sixth cervical vertebra (C6), the transverse process was bipartite with a broad ventral lamina, lacking the trifid configuration reported in gliding sciurids. CT-derived and dry skeletal caliper measurements were evaluated independently without assuming intermethod equivalence. Conclusion The present study provides a descriptive baseline characterization of the cervical vertebrae in the Persian squirrel using anatomical, radiographic, and CT approaches. The absence of a true body in C1, the morphology of C2-C5, and the bipartite transverse process of C6 represent notable anatomical features of this species. The obtained morphometric data may serve as preliminary anatomical information for future comparative and imaging studies.

title: Pretreatment Histopathology-Based Tumor Microenvironment Modeling Predicts Treatment-Specific Objective Responses in Non-small Cell Lung Cancer.
abstract: Accurate prediction of treatment response remains challenging in cancer. To facilitate response prediction in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), we developed PRISM, an interpretable multiscale graph-learning framework for estimating treatment-specific objective response from pretreatment H&E whole-slide images. PRISM integrated multiresolution tissue representations with a cell-level tumor microenvironment (TME) hypergraph, thereby treating higher-order microenvironmental organization as a learnable component of treatment-response prediction. Samples from 7,082 patients from four Chinese centers were screened. PRISM was evaluated across treatment specific cohorts receiving targeted therapy (T), EGFR-targeted therapy (T_EGFR), immune checkpoint inhibitor-based therapy (ICI), chemoimmunotherapy (CI), and chemotherapy (C) using patient-level internal cross-validation, independent multicenter external validation, and prospective silent validation. PRISM predicted early objective responses across prespecified systemic therapies in NSCLC. In comparison to 18 established multiple-instance learning and computational pathology baseline models, PRISM remained competitive, with numerical advantages in selected tasks. Multiscale attribution and exploratory H&E-derived TME analyses provided spatial context for model predictions. Overall, PRISM offers a morphology-based framework for estimating early response to prespecified systemic therapies and warrants further prospective multicenter evaluation.

title: Molecular Residual Disease After Definitive Chemoradiotherapy in Locally Advanced Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Value and Optimal Timing for ctDNA Assessment.
abstract: Background Accurate post-treatment assessment after definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) in locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (LA-HNSCC) remains challenging due to limitations of standard imaging. We evaluated the diagnostic performance, prognostic value and optimal timing of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for molecular residual disease (MRD) detection. Methods Seventy-four patients with LA-HNSCC treated with definitive CRT were prospectively enrolled. Plasma samples were collected before treatment, at 8 and 12 weeks after CRT, and during follow-up. ctDNA was analysed using a plasma-only methylation-based assay. Diagnostic performance for recurrence detection and associations with progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated and compared with 12-week PET/CT findings. Results Baseline ctDNA was detectable in 85.1% of patients. Among post-treatment timepoints, week-12 ctDNA showed the highest diagnostic accuracy for recurrence detection, with 69% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% positive predictive value, and 76% negative predictive value. Detectable week-12 ctDNA was associated with shorter PFS (HR, 6.44; 95% CI, 2.73-16.74; p<0.001) and OS (HR, 7.31; 95% CI, 2.80-22.31; p<0.001 ). Longitudinal ctDNA surveillance identified additional recurrences among patients with initially undetectable week-12 ctDNA. Exploratory analyses integrating PET/CT and ctDNA identified prognostically distinct PFS groups (log-rank P=0.033), with the greatest additional prognostic stratification observed among PET partial-responders. Conclusions Plasma-only methylation-based ctDNA provided high-specificity prognostic information after definitive CRT in LA-HNSCC, particularly at week 12 and in PET partial-responders. ctDNA may complement PET/CT for post-treatment risk stratification, but should not be used as a stand-alone test to exclude recurrence.

title: Tissue factor-specific sdAb radiotracers for molecular imaging in solid tumors.
abstract: Tissue factor (TF) expression has been associated with tumor aggressiveness and poor prognosis in several cancers. With the recent FDA approval of an antibody-drug-conjugate targeting TF, tisotumab vedotin for recurrent metastatic cervical cancer, companion diagnostic tools capable of capturing tumor heterogeneity are increasingly critical. In this study, we developed and characterized single domain antibody (sdAb)-based radiotracers to non-invasively visualize tumors expressing either murine (m) or human (h) TF protein. SdAbs targeting hTF and mTF were obtained from an immune llama library. Seven candidates targeting each species' orthologue were selected, characterized in vitro and radiolabeled with 99mTc for in vivo screening in athymic nude mice bearing both mTF and hTF positive tumors. Lead anti-hTF sdAb was radiolabeled with 68Ga for PET imaging. In vitro, all sdAbs exhibited excellent affinities for their respective targets, reaching the picomolar range. When radiolabeled with 99mTc, the lead compounds showed strong uptake and specific binding in TF-positive tumors as confirmed by SPECT imaging. The lead sdAb 64B4 targeting hTF protein, demonstrated an uptake of 8.07±1.02% IA/g in BxPC-3 tumors and a tumor-to-blood ratio of 26.06±4.36. The best candidate for targeting mTF protein, sdAb 66A12, displayed an uptake of 3.30±0.22% IA/g in mTF positive tumors and a tumor-to-blood ratio of 10.70±2.83. Off-tumor uptake was detected in several organs, with unexpectedly the highest levels detected in brown adipose tissue, consistent with mTF protein expression levels determined by ELISA. We successfully developed and validated sdAb-based radiotracers targeting either mTF or hTF, enabling the noninvasive visualization of TF-expressing tumors.

title: High-Resolution Intraoperative Guide for Cochlear Implant Surgery Using Optical Coherence Tomography.
abstract: Introduction Despite advances in soft surgery, intracochlear trauma during cochlear implant (CI) electrode insertion still occurs, potentially damaging cochlear microstructures and affecting hearing outcomes or future treatments. While the round window membrane (RWM) approach is generally less traumatic, the hook region's complex anatomy can still cause mechanical injury, often due to limited visual guidance. Preoperative imaging and intraoperative optical coherence tomography (OCT) could reduce trauma by offering high-resolution, real-time visualization of cochlear microstructures. Methods Eight fresh-frozen human temporal bones (TB1-TB8) were included. The first 6 specimens (TB1-TB6) underwent micro-CT scanning with manual segmentation to establish detailed anatomical baselines and served for OCT-micro-CT co-registration. Following a standard cochlear implantation approach, intracochlear structures behind the RWM were visualized using a microscope-integrated OCT system, with additional imaging performed via an anteroinferior cochleostomy to compare access routes. Electrode insertions were performed under OCT guidance in selected specimens, while feasibility of intraoperative workflow and insertion dynamics was assessed in TB7-TB8 under fluoroscopic control. Results OCT images were successfully obtained for each TB, with proper RWM exposure being crucial. The OCT microscope enabled scanning of the RWM and scala tympani (ST) from various axes, depths, and angles at a surgical working distance, improving assessment of proximal ST anatomy. OCT appears reliable for evaluating microanatomy through the RWM, guiding CI electrode selection, approach, and proximal array course modification during insertion. By visualizing critical structures and inferring deeper ones, it supports preoperative imagery-based planning and may reduce the risk of intracochlear damage. Conclusion Intraoperative OCT imaging enhances the precision of the cochlear opening site and electrode insertion axis. By integrating OCT, CI surgery could shift from a largely blind procedure to one with significant visual guidance, reducing surgical trauma and improving postoperative hearing preservation.

title: Non-detection in exfoliative airway cytology of lung cancer: associations with sampling context and reported lepidic morphology.
abstract: Introduction We examined whether unequivocally negative airway cytology was associated with sampling context and reported histopathological features in histologically confirmed lung cancers. Methods This retrospective cohort included selected linked accessions with histologically confirmed lung cancer and definitive exfoliative-airway cytology interpretations. Accessions containing intrapulmonary fine-needle aspiration were excluded. The full-cohort model excluded suspicious-only and unknown records and used patient-clustered robust standard errors. A co-primary analysis was restricted to adenocarcinomas without the institution-specific processing prefix because the opportunity to report lepidic growth varied with the histological material available. Three pathologists audited 300 report-text records. Results The selected linked cohort comprised 5,376 pathology accessions from 4,846 patient clusters; 1,388 (25.8%) were unequivocally negative. Detection proportions were 78.7% with brushing plus another airway sample, 67.9% with brushing alone, 45.1% with lavage/washing alone, and 18.5% with sputum alone; these are accession-level proportions within the selected cohort and are not overall diagnostic sensitivity estimates. A lepidic feature reported in the paired histopathology was associated with non-detection in the full cohort (odds ratio, 3.52; 95% confidence interval, 2.24-5.53) and in the ascertainment-restricted adenocarcinoma analysis (odds ratio, 3.05; 95% confidence interval, 1.82-5.14). When suspicious interpretations were counted as non-detection, the odds ratio was 3.44 (95% confidence interval, 2.25-5.26). Conclusion Sampling context and a reported lepidic feature were associated with non-detection in this selected cohort. The data cannot distinguish tumour biology from sampling, visibility, specimen adequacy, interpretive factors, or outcome-dependent availability of histological material, and do not establish comparative sampling effectiveness. They support cytology-histology audits stratified by specimen type, diagnostic category, and histological material.

title: MRI-Based Analysis of Post-HIFU Efficacy in Uterine Adenomyosis and Personalized Treatment Strategies.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the clinical outcomes of high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) ablation in patients with different subtypes of adenomyosis as classified by preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and to explore the implications for personalized treatment planning. Design A retrospective cohort study. Participants 447 patients with adenomyosis who underwent HIFU treatment were classified according to the Kishi MRI criteria into Type I (intrinsic, n=195), Type II (extrinsic, n=92), Type III (intramural, n=50), and Type IV (full-thickness, n=110). Methods All 447 patients underwent HIFU ablation under standardized procedural protocols.Treatment parameters, non-perfused volume (NPV) ratio, relief of dysmenorrhea (assessed by NRS score), and improvement in menstrual blood volume (assessed by FPS score) were analyzed and compared across subtypes at 3 and 6 months post-treatment. Results Patients with Type IV adenomyosis had significantly larger lesion volumes and required longer treatment durations with higher energy delivery (p<0.001). The NPV ratio was highest in Type I (74.91% ± 28.34%), followed by Type III (70.34% ± 26.12%), both significantly higher than in Type II (60.01% ± 2.9%) and Type IV (65.93% ± 25.41%) (p<0.05). All subtypes demonstrated significant and sustained improvement in both dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia at follow-up (p<0.05). The comprehensive treatment success rate was highest for Type IV at both 3 (21.82%) and 6 months (27.27%). Limitations This study has several limitations. First, the retrospective design inherently introduces selection bias and limits causal inference. Second,long-term follow-up beyond 6 months was not available, precluding assessment of durability of symptom relief and recurrence rates. Conclusions High-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) provides effective symptom relief for all MRI-classified subtypes of adenomyosis. Treatment parameters and efficacy, however, vary by subtype. MRI classification is therefore crucial for guiding treatment and anticipating technical challenges. A personalized approach based on subtype may further optimize therapeutic outcomes.

title: Ovarian cancer screening using serum CA125 and transvaginal ultrasound: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background The clinical utility of ovarian cancer screening remains unclear. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of serum cancer antigen 125 combined with transvaginal ultrasound in the early detection of ovarian cancer and the improvement of prognosis. Methods Systematically searched five electronic databases to identify eligible randomised controlled trials. The primary outcomes were ovarian cancer incidence and ovarian cancer-specific mortality. Results were evaluated using relative risks and 95% confidence intervals. Results Four randomised controlled trials were included in this meta-analysis, comprising 188147 participants in the screening group and 187394 in the control group. Pooled results showed no statistically significant difference in overall ovarian cancer incidence and ovarian cancer-specific mortality between the two groups (all p>0.05). Subgroup analysis further showed that the screening group had a significantly higher detection rate of Stage I ovarian cancer than the control group (relative risks=1.35, 95% confidence interval:1.14-1.60; p<0.001). For histological subtypes, the screening group had a significantly higher detection rate of serous carcinoma (relative risk=1.09, 95% confidence interval:1.01-1.19; p=0.030), but a significantly lower detection rate of mucinous carcinoma (relative risk=0.69, 95% confidence interval:0.51-0.94; p=0.020). No statistically significant difference was observed between the two groups in other subgroups (all p>0.05). Conclusion For asymptomatic women in the general population, combined serum cancer antigen 125 and transvaginal ultrasound screening should be approached with caution. Current evidence indicates that this screening strategy neither reduced​ the overall incidence of ovarian cancer nor improved​ overall survival, despite potentially increasing the detection rate of Stage I and early-stage serous carcinoma.

title: Macular Microcirculation by OCT-A in Relation to Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy and Ocular Surface Biomarkers: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate the association between diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), corneal sensitivity, and tear matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) with macular microcirculatory parameters assessed by optical coherence tomography angiography (OCT-A) in patients with diabetes mellitus. Methods This cross-sectional observational study included 158 eyes of 79 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) undergoing routine retinopathy screening at a single tertiary centre. Superficial capillary plexus vessel density and foveal avascular zone (FAZ) parameters (area, perimeter, and circularity index) were obtained by OCT-A (Cirrus 6000, AngioPlex®, Carl Zeiss Meditec). Corneal sensitivity was measured with the Brill esthesiometer and tear MMP-9 was assessed with the InflammaDry test. DPN was confirmed by electroneuromyography. Linear mixed models with random intercept per patient were applied to account for bilateral data. Results Among OCT-A parameters, vessel density and FAZ area and perimeter did not show significant association with DPN status, MMP-9 positivity, or corneal sensitivity. FAZ circularity showed a significant negative association with DPN in the multivariable model (β = -0.07; p = 0.021) and with corneal sensitivity in the linear mixed model (β = 0.01; p = 0.049), but was not associated with MMP-9 status (p = 0.691). No OCT-A parameter was associated with MMP-9 in any analysis. Conclusions FAZ circularity was independently associated with DPN and with reduced corneal sensitivity, suggesting a potential retinal correlate of neurovascular damage in diabetes; however, this is a model-dependent, exploratory finding requiring prospective confirmation. No OCT-A parameter was associated with MMP-9 status, suggesting compartmental dissociation between anterior segment inflammation and posterior segment microvascular status at this disease stage.

title: Myocardial Work Analysis: A Novel Echocardiographic Approach for Early Detection of Myocardial Fibrosis in Pediatric Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy With Preserved LVEF-A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background While myocardial work (MW) indices have shown diagnostic and prognostic value in various cardiovascular diseases, their role in detecting myocardial fibrosis in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) remains unexplored. This prospective study investigates MW's potential for early identification of fibrosis in pediatric DMD patients with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. Methods In this large prospective cohort, we enrolled 242 genetically confirmed DMD males (aged 6-18 years) with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50% by cardiac magnetic resonance and 54 age-matched controls. Comprehensive echocardiographic assessment included global work index, global constructive work, global wasted work, and global work efficiency analysis. Myocardial fibrosis was assessed via late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance at baseline at 1-year follow-up. Results Patients with DMD demonstrated significantly impaired MW indices versus controls (global work index, 1371.4±225.84 versus 1598.04±207.01 mm Hg%; global work efficiency, median 94.67% [Q1-Q3, 93.00-96.00] versus 95.33% [94.30-96.33]; global constructive work, 1630.34±246.37 versus 1900.22±195.84 mm Hg%; global wasted work, median 67.67 [Q1-Q3, 50.17-86.25] versus 59.00 [48.00-73.00] mm Hg%; all P <0.01). Notably, MW abnormalities preceded global longitudinal strain reduction, with significant differences even in patients with DMD with normal global longitudinal strain (≥18%). Global work efficiency showed moderate diagnostic accuracy for baseline late gadolinium enhancement (area under the curve, 0.618) and was associated with subsequent late gadolinium enhancement development in exploratory longitudinal analysis (area under the curve, 0.798; cutoff of 95.85%), providing complementary information beyond conventional echocardiographic parameters. Conclusions This large-scale prospective study suggests that MW analysis, particularly global work efficiency, might be useful for early detection of cardiac dysfunction and might be associated with short-term fibrosis in patients with DMD and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. However, given the limited number of progression events, this finding should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Prognostic Value of Left Ventricular Kinetic Energy Assessed by 4D Flow CMR in Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Prospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
abstract: Background Alterations in left ventricular intracavitary hemodynamics can occur early in the course of nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM). However, the association between 4-dimensional (4D) flow cardiac magnetic resonance parameters and adverse outcomes in patients with DCM remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate whether 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance parameters can predict adverse outcomes in patients with DCM. Methods In this multicenter prospective cohort study, 675 adult patients with DCM (mean age, 56 years; 399 men) from 3 medical centers and 80 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance. Left ventricular flow components and kinetic energy parameters were quantified. The primary end point was a composite of heart failure events, including heart failure-related death, unplanned heart failure hospitalization, or cardiac transplantation. Results During a median follow-up of 42 months, 58 patients (8.6%) experienced the primary end point. Compared with controls, patients with DCM exhibited reduced peak systolic kinetic energy normalized to EDV (KEi EDV ) and peak E-wave KEi EDV ; these differences were more pronounced in those who developed the primary end point. In univariable Cox regression, direct flow, residual volume, peak systolic KEi EDV , and peak E-wave KEi EDV were significant predictors of the primary end point (all P <0.05). After adjustment for left ventricular ejection fraction, NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), extracellular volume fraction, extent of late gadolinium enhancement, peak systolic KEi EDV (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.39 [95% CI, 0.28-0.53]), and peak E-wave KEi EDV (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.35 [95% CI, 0.26-0.48]) remained independently associated with the primary end point (both P <0.001). Furthermore, these 2 kinetic energy parameters provided incremental prognostic value beyond clinical markers and conventional imaging markers for predicting the primary end point. Conclusions In patients with DCM, decreased peak systolic KEi EDV and peak E-wave KEi EDV , as measured by 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance, are independently associated with poor prognosis and provide incremental prognostic value for risk stratification beyond clinical and conventional imaging markers. Furthermore, these 2 kinetic energy parameters provided incremental prognostic value beyond clinical markers and conventional imaging markers for predicting the primary end point.

Conclusions

In patients with DCM, decreased peak systolic KEiEDV and peak E-wave KEiEDV, as measured by 4D flow cardiac magnetic resonance, are independently associated with poor prognosis and provide incremental prognostic value for risk stratification beyond clinical and conventional imaging markers.

title: Myocardial Responses to Eplontersen in Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: The CARDIO-TTRansform CMR study.
abstract: Background Transthyretin-lowering therapies target the underlying cause of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), but their effects on myocardial amyloid burden and cardiac remodelling remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated the myocardial effects of sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen using serial multiparametric cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). Methods This CMR study was a pre-specified, international, prospective study embedded within the randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 CARDIO-TTRansform trial. Participants underwent CMR at baseline and planned assessments at weeks 25, 49, 97, and 140. The primary imaging analysis evaluated longitudinal changes in CMR parameters using mixed models for repeated measures. Myocardial amyloid regression and progression were defined as ≥5 percentage-point decreases and increases in extracellular volume (ECV), respectively. All other patients were considered stable. Results We enrolled 120 participants with baseline and ≥1 follow-up CMR assessment (eplontersen, n=58; placebo, n=62; mean age, 76.7±6.5 years; 95% male; baseline stabilizer, 12.5%). At week 140 eplontersen resulted in lower ECV, compared with placebo (least-squares mean difference [95% CI], -6.7 percentage points [ -8.7 to -4.7]; P<0.001) and lower native T1 ( -25.9ms [-41.7 to -10.2 ]; P=0.002) and left ventricular mass (-19.1g [-28.0 to -10.2]; P<0.001). Eplontersen also increased left ventricular ejection fraction (+5.1% [1.8-8.3]; P=0.002), right ventricular ejection fraction (+4.6% [0.6-8.7]; P=0.03), and left ventricular global longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain and right ventricular longitudinal strain (all P<0.05), compared to placebo. At week-140, myocardial amyloid regression occurred in 12.5% receiving eplontersen versus 0% receiving placebo, whereas progression occurred in 12.5% versus 76%, respectively. Conclusions Sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen resulted in substantially lower myocardial ECV and favorable changes in cardiac structure, biventricular systolic function, and myocardial deformation compared with placebo in a cohort of patients mostly not on background stabilizer at baseline. These findings provide randomized evidence that lowering circulating transthyretin modifies myocardial disease progression in ATTR-CM and support serial multiparametric CMR for characterizing myocardial treatment response.

title: Risk Stratification and Outcomes of Right Atrial Phasic Function in Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy: A Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Study.
abstract: Background Advanced arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is associated with a high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias (MVA) and end-stage heart failure (HF). However, the prognostic role of right atrial (RA) mechanics, as quantified by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), remains largely unexplored. Methods Consecutive patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy undergoing CMR between 2014 and 2021 were retrospectively included. Demographics, clinical history, and strain parameters were collected. The primary clinical end points were end-stage HF and MVA. Results A total of 316 patients (mean age 38±15 years; 66.1% men) were included. Over a median follow-up of 5.3 years, 49 developed end-stage HF and 103 experienced MVA outcomes. Multivariable Cox and Fine-Gray models showed that impaired RA reservoir strain was an independent predictor of end-stage HF (hazard ratio [HR] 0.92, 95% CI 0.89-0.96, P <0.001) and MVA outcomes (subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) 0.98, 95% CI 0.96-0.99, P =0.025), with added prognostic value beyond clinical and imaging variables, improving the C-statistic to 0.84 and 0.70, respectively. Kaplan-Meier survival curves indicated that RA reservoir strain <18.6% was associated with higher end-stage HF risk, consistent across subgroups regardless of left ventricular involvement (both log-rank P <0.05). The association between RA reservoir strain <23.0% and MVA was significant in the overall cohort ( P <0.001) and in patients without left ventricular involvement ( P =0.002), but not in those with left ventricular involvement ( P =0.08). Conclusions Lower cardiac magnetic resonance-derived RA reservoir strain was independently associated with end-stage HF and MVA in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and provided incremental prognostic value beyond conventional risk markers. These findings support RA mechanics as a potential complementary component of multichamber CMR risk assessment, pending external validation.

title: Standardized Ultrafast Transcranial Ultrasound Acquisition in Acute Stroke: The HYPER-AI-SCAN Pilot Study With Exploratory Artificial Intelligence Analysis.
abstract: Background Intracerebral hemorrhage requires rapid mechanism-specific treatment, yet early stroke triage relies on clinical severity scales that do not reliably distinguish hemorrhage from ischemic stroke. We assessed the feasibility of a standardized ultrafast transcranial ultrasound protocol designed to support subsequent artificial intelligence (AI)-based intracerebral hemorrhage detection. Methods HYPER-AI-SCAN (Hyper-Acute AI-Assisted Sonographic Cerebral Hemorrhage Assessment Network) was a single-center prospective feasibility study with embedded exploratory AI analysis. Between March and December 2025, 102 adults with acute computed tomography (CT)-confirmed stroke were prospectively enrolled according to trained operator availability. Primary feasibility outcomes were protocol completion, operator-rated adequate transtemporal windows, and acquisition time. In patients with retrievable paired baseline CT, exploratory AI analyses compared CT-only, ultrasound-only, and cross-modal CT-guided ultrasound models using patient-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, and specificity. Results Two patients were excluded after acquisition because insonation depth was <19 cm, yielding 100 evaluable patients (33 intracerebral hemorrhage; 67 ischemic stroke). The protocol was completed in all evaluable patients; adequate transtemporal windows were identified in 87%, and median acquisition time was 22 seconds (interquartile range, 13-31). Paired baseline CT images were available in 91 patients. Mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.86 (SD, 0.07) for the CT-only model, 0.85 (SD, 0.14) for the ultrasound-only model, and 0.92 (SD, 0.07) for the cross-modal model. Conclusions Standardized ultrafast transcranial ultrasound acquisition was feasible at the bedside in acute stroke and generated brief cine-loops suitable for exploratory AI development. Multicenter external validation is required before diagnostic or triage application. Registration information Clinicaltrials.gov. Identifier: NCT07319013.
